temples.name: Shri Radha Raman Mandir
temples.builtYear: Deity self-manifested 1542 (Gopala Bhatta Goswami); the PRESENT temple building completed 1826, patron Shah Kundan Lal (same patron family as Shahji Mandir, 1876)
temples.material: Plain dressed sandstone, unpainted and uncarved over most surfaces; one red sandstone archway as an accent; the surrounding compound houses are lime-plastered brick, 2 storeys
temples.primaryColour: Light brown / buff sandstone (warm pale tan, NOT the deep red of the Akbar-period temples)
temples.accentColour: Deep red sandstone at the revelation-spot archway; embossed silver at the sanctum doors; whitewash/pale ochre plaster on the surrounding Goswami houses
temples.approxFootprintM: NOT DOCUMENTED. The temple block is small — an eyewitness description calls it 'wedged in between a couple of buildings'. For modelling, treat the shrine block as roughly 12-18 m frontage and the whole Radharaman Ghera complex as two successive courtyards, each on the order of 20-30 m across, ringed by houses.
temples.towerForm: CONFLICTING SOURCES — resolve in favour of the eyewitness account. The detailed description is of 'a simple sandstone structure at first glance hardly distinguishable from the houses around it', i.e. a low haveli-type block with no monumental tower. Generic tourism/SEO pages claim 'Nagara style with towering shikhara, dome-shaped roof and gold-plated spire' — that text is unsourced boilerplate and contradicts the first-hand description. Model it as a low flat-roofed masonry block, at most a modest superstructure over the sanctum; do NOT give it a soaring shikhara.
temples.facade: Main archway decorated with spiralling lotus designs. The antechamber front is three CUSPED (multifoil) arches in unpainted sandstone — this is the single most reliable facade fact and the thing you actually see at darshan. No documented jali screens, balconies or figural carved bands on the temple front. The courtyards are enclosed by plain two-storey houses whose height 'shuts out direct sunlight'.
temples.entrance: Sequence, not a single gate. From the street: an archway, then a MASSIVE doorway with heavy wooden doors that are closed at night, into the first courtyard. A small passage on the left just inside that gate leads to a red sandstone archway and a shrine marking the spot where Radharaman revealed himself, with a tree beside it (where the basket of shalagramas is said to have hung). Another passageway off the first courtyard leads to the memorial shrine of Gopala Bhatta and the deceased Goswamis. Straight across the first courtyard, a second massive doorway with heavy wooden doors opens into the second courtyard, which holds the temple.
temples.roofline: NOT DOCUMENTED in any reliable source. No documented chhatris, kalasha, finials or flag. Do not invent a gold spire.
temples.compound: Walled compound called Radharaman Ghera, entered from the street; TWO successive enclosed courtyards, the first lined with the houses of the Goswami families, the second holding the temple. Behind the main temple, reached by a narrow passageway, stand the small building originally built for Radharaman in the late 16th century plus a somewhat larger one beside it — both very plain — now used as the deity's kitchen, dining room and bedroom. A fire has been kept burning in a TEN-FOOT-LONG fire pit in that old building since Gopala Bhatta's time; all the deity's food is cooked from it.
temples.distinguishing: You cannot see it coming. There is no forecourt, no skyline, no approach view — it is a wooden-doored gateway in a street wall, a dark house-lined courtyard, then a second gate, then a plain sandstone front with three cusped arches and a silver door. Inside: a deity under twelve inches tall with NO Radha beside him, only her emblem. And behind the temple, a ten-foot fire trench that has never been allowed to go out in ~480 years.
temples.interior: A raised platform serves as the antechamber to the inner sanctum, fronted by the three cusped unpainted-sandstone arches; at the rear an embossed silver double-leaved door leads into the sanctum. The deity stands FACING EAST, so pilgrims stand west of him looking east. Two sets of stairs formerly let pilgrims go up onto the platform for close darshan; these were removed after the Temple Entry Act, and now only Goswamis and temple servants go up. Lighting: courtyard daylight is largely blocked by the two-storey houses, so the interior reads as dim, lamp-and-chandelier lit against pale stone and bright silver.
temples.deityDescription: Radha Raman: a svayambhu (self-manifested) deity that emerged from a shalagrama-shila, therefore BLACK/dark stone with a natural glossy shalagram surface — the shalagram markings are still visible on his back and are shown at his appearance-day abhisheka. 'Not more than twelve inches in height' (~30 cm). Standing tribhanga (three-fold bending) flute-playing form. Tradition says he combines the lotus face of Govind Dev, the chest of Gopinath and the lotus feet of Madan Mohan. CRITICAL: there is NO Radha murti in this temple. A representation/emblem of Shri Radha (commonly described as her crown) is placed reverentially on Radharaman's left. Dressed and ornamented daily by the Goswamis; on Dussehra he is placed on a large silver elephant, and a silver jhula is used at Hariyali Teej. Specific everyday jewellery/dress is not documented in text — observe published photographs rather than invent.
temples.confidence: medium-high for compound sequence, entrance, cusped-arch antechamber, silver doors, deity and fire pit; LOW for height, footprint, roofline and tower form (genuinely undocumented)
temples.sources: Vrindavan Today, 'The marvelous history and rituals of Shri Radharaman temple' (detailed eyewitness-style description of the Ghera, courtyards, arches, silver door, fire pit, deity height); The Hare Krishna Movement, 'The Seven Goswami Temples of Vrindavan' (1826 completion, Shah Kundan Lal, light brown sandstone facade, spiralling lotus archway, two courtyards); Wikipedia 'Radha Raman Temple, Vrindavan' (founding, shalagrama origin, tribhanga form — no architecture). Growse's 1883 memoir does NOT describe this temple. Approx location (OpenStreetMap): 27.5854 N, 77.6987 E, in the lanes between Nidhivan and Kesi Ghat.

temples.name: Shri Radha Damodar Mandir
temples.builtYear: Founded 1542 by Jiva Goswami at Seva Kunj; deities taken to Jaipur c.1670 and returned 1739; the PRESENT fabric is reported as roughly 250 years old, i.e. later 18th century
temples.material: Humble masonry — lime-plastered brick, with BARE BRICK now exposed where the plaster/facade has crumbled. Checkered marble paving to the interior floors. No monumental dressed-stone architecture. Growse (1883) dismissed Vrindavan's smaller temples of this class: 'Though of ancient date, they have been often renewed and possess no special architectural merit.'
temples.primaryColour: Weathered cream/ochre lime plaster with patches of exposed red-brown brick; pale grey-and-white checkered marble underfoot
temples.accentColour: Green of the tulasi in the courtyard; dark stone of the deities; saffron/red cloth
temples.approxFootprintM: NOT DOCUMENTED. Known relative fact: the courtyard is SMALLER than Radha Shyamsundar's. Model a tight courtyard on the order of 12-18 m across with the altar block on one side, surrounded by the samadhi courts and a narrow rectangular circulation corridor.
temples.towerForm: Flat-roofed / low haveli-courtyard type. No monumental nagara shikhara, no gopuram, no dome of any scale. The vertical incident comes from the small samadhi shrines (compact square chhatri-like tomb structures), not from the temple itself.
temples.facade: The altar front carries THREE ARCHES (this is the diagnostic contrast: Radha Shyamsundar two minutes away has FIVE). Plain plastered wall surfaces otherwise; crumbling render exposing brick. No documented jali screens, carved bands or balconies.
temples.entrance: A gateway off Nikunj Gali / the Seva Kunj lane in Loi Bazar leads directly into the courtyard that fronts the altar. Modest scale, no torana, no monumental steps.
temples.roofline: Low and broken — plain parapets over the shrine, with the domed/pyramidal caps of the samadhi shrines rising around the courts. Not documented in detail.
temples.compound: Walled, and this is the point of the place: it is a compound of TOMBS, not a temple with a forecourt. Courtyard with a tulasi that pilgrims circumambulate. Rear and northern courtyards described as a 'courtyard of one hundred samadhis' with tombs in rows — including the samadhi and bhajan-kutir of Rupa Goswami, the samadhi of Jiva Goswami, the samadhi of Krishnadasa Kaviraja, and many pushpa-samadhis of other Vaishnavas. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada's rooms are in the northern compound. A narrow internal PARIKRAMA walkway runs between the buildings; four circuits of it are held equal to one parikrama of Govardhan Hill, so the corridor is in constant slow-moving use. A well dug by Rupa Goswami survives on that path.
temples.distinguishing: A tiny, shabby, plaster-peeling courtyard that is one of the most walked-in places in Vrindavan — because of the narrow rectangular corridor between the buildings that pilgrims circle four times, and because the courts around it are packed with the small tombs of the Goswamis. Plus the Giriraj shila: a Govardhan stone bearing a footprint, flute, stick and cow's hoofprint, kept behind a curtain and produced on request.
temples.interior: Simple covered altar hall behind three arches. The simhasana (altar throne) carries FOUR sets of Radha-Krishna murtis side by side: Radha-Damodara (the presiding pair), Radha-Vrindavanchandra (Krishnadasa Kaviraja's), Radha-Madhava, and Radha-Chhailchikan (Bhugarbha Goswami's), plus additional pratibhu-murtis. A room to the left of the altar is traditionally pointed out as Jiva Goswami's library. Marble checkerboard floor, stones worn smooth by handling. Lighting is low and interior — lamps and small chandeliers against plastered walls.
temples.deityDescription: Radha-Damodara: an EIGHT-INCH (~20 cm) deity carved by Rupa Goswami from a piece of BLACK stone from the Vindhya mountains, in the month of Kartik/Damodar. The deities here are black stone, unlike the marble deities of some other Vrindavan temples. Radharani stands on Damodar's LEFT and Lalita Sakhi on his RIGHT. Dressed in the usual Braj manner with turban/crown, garlands and metal ornaments; specific daily dress is not documented in text. NOTE A SOURCE CONFLICT: one travel source describes the presiding Damodar as a 'five-foot black marble deity' — that is inconsistent with the eight-inch black-stone account given by multiple Gaudiya sources and should not be used. Also note the tradition dispute: some sources say the original went to Jaipur and a pratibhu-murti is worshipped here; others say the deities returned from Jaipur in 1739. Do not resolve this in the model — it makes no visual difference.
temples.confidence: medium — layout, samadhi courts, three arches, parikrama corridor, four deity sets and the 8-inch black-stone deity are all multiply attested; building height, footprint, roof and exact material are not documented
temples.sources: Wikipedia 'Radha Damodar Temple, Vrindavan' (1542, Jiva Goswami, Jaipur 1670/return 1739, deity list, Giriraj shila, four-rounds tradition); mathura.nic.in official district page; Braj Ras (brajrasik.org) article (Nikunj Lane, bhajan-kutir and samadhis in the courtyard, Giriraj Charan Shila with footprint/flute/stick/hoofprint); Vrindavan Forest, 'Sri Sri Radha Damodar Temple' (exposed brick, ~250-year-old fabric, courtyard of samadhis, four deity sets, checkered marble, Giriraj behind a curtain); The Gaudiya Treasures of Bengal (black stone from the Vindhyas 1542; Radha left, Lalita right); The Hare Krishna Movement, 'Seven Goswami Temples' (three arches vs Shyamsundar's five; Rupa Goswami's well); Growse, 'Mathura: A District Memoir' (1883) p.257 — records only the samadhis, and explicitly says the smaller Vrindavan temples have 'no special architectural merit'. Approx location (OSM): 27.5838 N, 77.6956 E.

temples.name: Shri Radha Gopinath Mandir
temples.builtYear: OLD temple c.1580-1590 (Growse: possibly the earliest of the four Akbar-period series), founder Rai Sal (Raesil) Ji 'Darbari', a Shekhawat Kachhwaha noble of Akbar's court. NEW living temple built c.1819-1821 by a Bengali patron named in sources as Nanda Kumar (Ghos/Basu), the same patron as the new Madan Mohan temple.
temples.material: OLD: red sandstone (the imperial-grade Bharatpur/Rupbas type used for the four great Vrindavan temples), boldly moulded and carved. NEW: plain haveli-type masonry, plastered — not documented in detail.
temples.primaryColour: Deep warm red sandstone, now grey-brown with age, lichen and soot on the old temple; pale plaster on the newer temple grafted onto its north side
temples.accentColour: Carved stone terrace front and arabesque-carved choir arch; modern temple interiors carry painted rasa-lila murals
temples.approxFootprintM: Growse states the old temple 'corresponds very closely both in style and DIMENSIONS with that of Madan Mohan', whose measured plan is: nave 57 ft (17.4 m) long, choir 20 ft (6.1 m) square at the west end, sanctuary of the same 20 ft square beyond — i.e. roughly 29-30 m overall east-west by about 6-7.5 m wide, plus a tower-crowned chapel attached to the SOUTH side of the sacrarium. At Madan Mohan the nave's total height was only about 22 ft (6.7 m). The nave at Gopinath has entirely disappeared, so the STANDING footprint today is the choir + sanctuary block, roughly 6 m x 12-13 m, plus the south terrace/arcade.
temples.towerForm: RUINED / TRUNCATED curvilinear nagara shikhara. Growse, 1883: 'the nave has entirely disappeared; the three towers have been levelled with the roof; and the entrance gateway of the court-yard is tottering to its fall.' What survives and is described today is an 'almost pyramidal' red sandstone dome/tower stub standing slightly higher than the surrounding dwellings. At the parallel Madan Mohan the sanctuary tower is 'a plain octagon of curvilinear outline tapering towards the summit' — that is the form to truncate here.
temples.facade: The signature element is a CURIOUS ARCADE OF THREE BRACKET ARCHES on the SOUTH wall — Growse notes it serves no structural purpose and is purely an ornamental screen applied to a wall that already had a fine boldly moulded plinth. The terrace on which that arcade stands has a carved stone front (Growse excavated it out of accumulated ground level in 1875). Bracket (corbelled) arches, not true arches — flat-ish lobed profiles carried on projecting brackets. Bold horizontal plinth mouldings. The choir arch is 'of handsome design, elaborately decorated with arabesque sculptures'.
temples.entrance: Principal entrance at the EAST end (standard for this series). A walled courtyard with its own gateway — described by Growse in 1883 as 'tottering to its fall'. At the closely-related Madan Mohan, the courtyard is entered after ascending a flight of steps through a massive square gateway with a pyramidal tower, which groups with the temple towers; use that as the model for the lost Gopinath gate.
temples.roofline: Flat terraced roof with the tower stubs levelled down to roof height; heavy moulded cornice and plinth bands. No documented chhatris, kalasha or flag on the old temple.
temples.compound: Walled courtyard with a ruinous gateway; the old temple is hemmed in and largely obscured by dense two-to-three-storey housing, so only the truncated tower reads above the rooftops. The new living temple is built hard against the NORTH side of the old one, blocking it. In Growse's time the interior of the old temple was in use as a stable and mean sheds had been built against the choir arch (he had them pulled down). Ownership today is contested: the Goswami family asserts private ownership, while UP State Archaeology attempted an 'Adopt a Heritage' handover in 2023 — it is NOT straightforwardly an ASI-run site like Govind Dev and Madan Mohan.
temples.distinguishing: The truncated, almost pyramidal red sandstone tower that just clears the rooftops and is the only way to find the place; the blind three-bracket-arch arcade stuck on the south wall like a screen; and the fact that a plain, busy living temple is welded onto the north flank of a gutted Mughal-era monument, so a visitor walks from working worship straight into a roofless ruin.
temples.interior: OLD: the plan is choir + sanctuary (each ~6 m square, formerly domed/vaulted) with a lateral chapel on the south, entered through a richly carved arabesque choir arch; the nave that once fronted it is gone, so the surviving interior is a tall, bare, top-lit stone chamber. NEW: haveli type — a covered altar hall facing a courtyard, with a rasa-lila mural painted on the temple wall and a large drum played during worship (single-source, treat as medium-low confidence).
temples.deityDescription: The present Radha-Gopinath deities are PRATIBHU (non-different replacement) murtis, installed 1748 after the originals were taken to Jaipur early in the 18th century; the original Gopinath is traditionally the deity of Vajranabha, rediscovered at Vamsivat by Paramananda (Padmanabha) Bhattacharya and worshipped by Madhu Pandit Goswami. ALTAR ARRANGEMENT IS THE UNIQUE FEATURE: Gopinath stands centre with ANANGA-MANJARI (identified with Jahnava Thakurani) on his LEFT and Radharani on his RIGHT, with Lalita and Vishakha flanking — the only Vrindavan altar to carry Ananga Manjari. Deity material, colour and size are NOT reliably documented; do not guess. Samadhi of Madhu Pandit near the temple's east side.
temples.confidence: HIGH for the old temple's fabric, plan, dimensions-by-analogy, the three-bracket-arch arcade and its ruined state (F.S. Growse, first-hand, with measurements); MEDIUM for the new temple and the altar arrangement; LOW for present heights and for the new temple's material
temples.sources: F.S. Growse, 'Mathura: A District Memoir' (1883), pp.251-254 — full text at archive.org/details/b29352095, downloaded and read directly: the Gopinath passage (founder Raesil Darbari; 'corresponds very closely both in style and dimensions with that of Madan Mohan'; ruined nave; three towers levelled; tottering courtyard gateway; the three-bracket-arch ornamental arcade; moulded plinth; carved terrace front he uncovered; arabesque choir arch; interior used as a stable; modern temple built c.1821 by the Bengali Kayastha Nand Kumar Ghos) and the Madan Mohan passage (nave 57 ft, choir 20 ft square, sanctuary same, nave height ~22 ft, sanctuary tower 'a plain octagon of curvilinear outline', south chapel, courtyard entered up steps through a massive square gateway with pyramidal tower). Rana Safvi, 'Gopinath Mandir in Vrindavan' (almost pyramidal red sandstone dome rising above surrounding dwellings; new haveli-type temple beside it). Braj Ras (brajrasik.org) 'Radha Gopinath Temple, Vrindavan' (Parikrama Marg at Kesi Ghat; altar arrangement; Madhu Pandit samadhi). ISKCON Desire Tree (Ananga Manjari on the altar; pratibhu deities in the new temple). Vrindavan Today, 'Potra Kund and Gopinath Temple handed over to private parties' (ownership dispute, state archaeology, Adopt-a-Heritage). Approx location (OSM): 27.5861 N, 77.6996 E, Parikrama Marg near Kesi Ghat.

temples.name: Shri Radha Shyamsundar Mandir
temples.builtYear: Founded by Shyamananda Pandit (17th century); the large deities were carved and installed on Vasanta Panchami 1719 by Baladeva Vidyabhushana. Present building fabric is undated in available sources.
temples.material: DARK RED SANDSTONE, plainly handled; exterior repeatedly described as 'very modest'. Stone donor plaques set into the fabric, inscribed in ODIA script.
temples.primaryColour: Dark red / maroon-brown sandstone, weathered
temples.accentColour: Green tulasi in the courtyard; ashta-dhatu (eight-metal alloy) gold-bronze of the Radha deity against the black stone of Shyamsundar
temples.approxFootprintM: NOT DOCUMENTED. Known relative fact: the courtyard is A BIT LARGER than Radha Damodar's (which is itself small). Model perhaps 18-25 m across, with the altar block on one side.
temples.towerForm: Flat-roofed haveli-courtyard type; no monumental shikhara, gopuram or dome is documented. Vertical incident comes from the samadhi shrine and the small Vrinda Devi shrine in the courtyard.
temples.facade: The altar front carries FIVE ARCHES — the diagnostic contrast with Radha Damodar's three, and the quickest way to tell the two apart in a model. Otherwise plain dark red sandstone walls. Donor plaques in Odia script are set about the fabric. No documented jali, balconies or carved figural bands.
temples.entrance: A modest doorway off the lane in Mohalla Seva Kunj near Loi Bazaar, on the same street as Radha Damodar (about a two-minute walk). Directly OPPOSITE the entrance door, across the courtyard, stands the samadhi of Shyamananda Prabhu — so the tomb is the first thing framed as you come in.
temples.roofline: Not documented. No recorded chhatris, kalasha or flag.
temples.compound: Walled courtyard, larger than Radha Damodar's, with tulasi growing in it. In the courtyard: a small Vrinda Devi shrine, and near it an UNDERGROUND bhajan-sthali — described as the original cave where Shyamananda worshipped the small Lala-Lali deities. Shyamananda Prabhu's samadhi faces the entrance; the pushpa-samadhi of Baladeva Vidyabhushana is behind the altar. The Nupur Prapti Sthala (where Radha's anklet was found) is a few metres from the temple.
temples.distinguishing: A plain dark-red sandstone courtyard temple whose altar is unmistakably FIVE arches wide, with three different-sized sets of deities standing together on one altar — a tall black-stone Krishna beside a golden metal Radha, and beside them a pair of tiny original deities too small to dress fully. Plus donor plaques in ODIA script all over the place: this is an Odia foundation in the middle of Braj, and the Puri connection is visible in the stonework. It is also the temple where mangala-arati is said to have first begun in Vrindavan, and has run uninterrupted since.
temples.interior: Covered altar hall behind five arches, facing the courtyard. THREE deity sets stand on the altar: the tall pair in the centre; the small original 'Lala-Lali' pair, which generally sit on the LEFT of the tall deities; and Radha Kunjabihari on the RIGHT side of the altar. An underground bhajan chamber is accessible in the courtyard. Lighting is courtyard-daylight at the arches falling off quickly into a dim altar recess.
temples.deityDescription: Shyamsundar (the large central deity): carved from a large NILA-SHILA (black stone) block from Nilgiri, near Shyamananda's birthplace village Athantar in Odisha — so a dark, near-black polished stone figure. His Radharani is cast in ASHTA-DHATU (eight-metal alloy) — i.e. a warm gold-bronze metal figure, visually a strong contrast with the black stone Krishna. Both installed on the central altar on Vasanta Panchami 1719 under Baladeva Vidyabhushana, who had them made precisely because the original deities were too small to be dressed in a full range of outfits and ornaments. The original small Shyamsundar (tradition: manifested from Radharani's heart at Seva Kunj / gifted by her to Shyamananda) and his Radha — together called Lala-Lali or 'small Radha-Shyamsundar' — are still on the altar, shortest of the three sets. A third set, Radha Kunjabihari (said to have been excavated at Nandagaon), stands on the right. Daily dress and ornament are not documented in text; work from published photographs, do not invent.
temples.confidence: medium — deity materials, altar composition, five arches, courtyard features and Odia plaques are well attested; building height, footprint, roofline and date of the present fabric are NOT documented
temples.sources: The Gaudiya Treasures of Bengal, 'Radha Shyamsundar Temple, Vrindavan — Founded by Shyamananda Pandit' (Mohalla Seva Kunj near Loi Bazaar, same road as Radha Damodar; nila-shila from Nilgiri, Odisha; ashta-dhatu Radha; Vasanta Panchami 1719; Radha Kunjabihari on the right; small originals cannot be widely dressed). Vrindavan Forest, 'Sri Sri Radha Shyamsundar Temple' (dark red sandstone; modest exterior; courtyard larger than Radha Damodar's with tulasi; FIVE arches; Shyamananda's samadhi opposite the entrance door; Odia-script donor plaques, mostly Puri donors). The Hare Krishna Movement, 'Seven Goswami Temples' (three arches at Radha Damodar vs five here). Tirthayatra.org (three deity sets; Lala-Lali shortest, on the left; bhajan kutir cave; Baladeva's pushpa-samadhi behind the altar; Nupur Prapti Sthala). VrajVrindavan.com (underground bhajan sthali near the small Vrinda Devi temple in the courtyard). ISKCON Desire Tree (first temple to begin mangala-arati). Approx location (OSM): 27.5826 N, 77.6959 E.

temples.name: Shri Jugal Kishore Mandir
temples.builtYear: The monument: Sambat 1684 = 1627 CE, in the reign of Jahangir; founder recorded as Non-Karan / Nau-Karan, said to be a Chauhan Thakur (Growse suspects he was Rai Sal's elder brother). The SEPARATE living Nimbarka-sampradaya Shri Yugal Kishor temple near Jugal Ghat is estimated at 300-400 years old, undated.
temples.material: Red sandstone throughout — the fourth and last of the four Akbar/Jahangir-period imperial-permission red sandstone temples of Vrindavan (after Govind Dev, Madan Mohan and Gopinath). Fine bracket carving, pierced stone tracery.
temples.primaryColour: Deep red sandstone, now heavily weathered to grey-brown and blackened by soot and river damp
temples.accentColour: Pierced tracery (jali) in the head of the choir arch reading pale against shadow; elephant-carved brackets
temples.approxFootprintM: MEASURED BY GROWSE: the choir is 25 FEET SQUARE (7.6 m), slightly larger than the 20 ft choirs of Madan Mohan and Gopinath. The nave has been COMPLETELY DESTROYED, so the standing footprint is essentially that ~7.6 m square choir/sanctuary block on its plinth. Original overall length, if it followed the series (nave ~57 ft + choir + sanctuary), would have been on the order of 28-32 m east-west.
temples.towerForm: Curvilinear nagara-type shikhara — and importantly a HOLLOW, MULTI-LEVEL one: Growse records clearing 'an accumulation of pigeons' dung more than four feet deep' from the UPPER ROOM OF THE TOWER, so there is a usable chamber inside the spire above the sanctum. He explicitly groups 'the towers of Madan Mohan and Jugal Kishor at Brinda-ban of the 16th [century]' as a stage in the development of the sikhara from the stupa: a square (occasionally octagonal) lower storey, a high curvilinear roof, and a pinnacle on a distinctive base. Model the lower storey square, the tower curvilinear in profile tapering to a pinnacle.
temples.facade: The diagnostic details are at the doors. Principal entrance at the EAST end as usual, but UNIQUELY in this group there are ALSO small doorways on BOTH NORTH AND SOUTH, each set under a projecting hood carried on EIGHT CLOSELY-SET BRACKETS CARVED INTO THE FORM OF ELEPHANTS. The choir arch is 'an interesting composition with a fan-light, so to speak, of PIERCED TRACERY in the head of the arch, and a group above representing KRISHNA SUPPORTING THE GOBARDHAN HILL'. Expect the bold moulded plinth and heavy horizontal string courses common to the series.
temples.entrance: Main door east, on axis; plus the two small hooded side doors on elephant brackets, north and south. No documented torana or monumental flight of steps at this temple specifically.
temples.roofline: Flat terraced roof over the lost nave line, the curvilinear tower rising from the choir/sanctuary block with an amalaka-and-finial pinnacle. Individual finials, kalasha and flags are not documented — do not invent gilding.
temples.compound: Stands at the LOWER (northern) end of the town, immediately by Kesi Ghat on the Yamuna bank — so unlike the other four Goswami temples it has an open river frontage and reads against water and sky rather than against houses. Growse in the 1870s had the building cleared and the municipality rent it for a rupee a month to keep it clean and empty for visitors; that arrangement was cancelled after he left and it reverted to use as a cattle shed. Its later history is that the deity was removed to Panna (Madhya Pradesh), where Raja Hindupat Singh built the Jugal Kishore temple during 1758-1778; the Vrindavan structure is widely reported as empty and locked by the ASI today, and a 2026 feature describes it as 'structurally fragile and almost entirely uninterpreted'.
temples.distinguishing: A red sandstone shell standing directly above Kesi Ghat with its whole nave gone — you walk up to a tall, roofless-fronted, square sanctum block with a curvilinear tower, and the two things you cannot miss are the row of eight little carved ELEPHANTS bracketing each side door hood, and the pierced-stone fanlight over the choir arch with Krishna lifting Govardhan carved above it. It is the temple you see from the river, not from the bazaar.
temples.interior: A single tall stone chamber 25 ft square, formerly vaulted, entered through the carved choir arch with its tracery fanlight; a further chamber inside the tower above. The nave that once preceded it is gone, so daylight now floods a space that was designed to be dim. In Growse's day the interior was empty and had been used as a cattle shed; there is no documented functioning altar, pillared hall or lighting scheme inside the monument.
temples.deityDescription: THE MONUMENT IS EMPTY — the original Jugal Kishore deity was removed to escape desecration and is worshipped at Panna, Madhya Pradesh, where Raja Hindupat Singh built a temple for it (reign 1758-1778). No documented deity in the Kesi Ghat structure. Living worship of Yugal Kishor in Vrindavan happens at the SEPARATE Nimbarka-sampradaya Shri Yugal Kishor temple near Jugal Ghat, on the way from Parikrama Marg to the Radha Vallabh temple; it holds Shri Yugal Kishor plus a second murti, Shri Jugal Bihari, who is taken out in a palanquin once a year. Material, size and dress of those deities are NOT documented.
temples.confidence: HIGH for the 1627 monument's fabric, the 25 ft choir, the elephant-bracket side doors, the tracery fanlight and Govardhan group, and the ruined nave (Growse, first-hand, measured); MEDIUM for its present condition and ASI lock; MEDIUM for the separate Nimbarka temple. NOTE A CONFLICT TO RESOLVE BEFORE MODELLING: several tourism/SEO pages describe the Kesi Ghat temple as an active temple with daily aarti and a tall intact shikhara. That is almost certainly a conflation with the living Nimbarka Yugal Kishor temple near Jugal Ghat. Treat them as TWO buildings.
temples.sources: F.S. Growse, 'Mathura: A District Memoir' (1883), p.254 — read directly from the archive.org full text (b29352095_djvu.txt): Sambat 1684 / 1627 AD, Jahangir's reign, founder Non-Karan; choir 25 feet square; principal entrance east; small north and south doorways under hoods on eight closely-set elephant brackets; nave completely destroyed; choir arch with pierced-tracery fanlight and Krishna-Govardhan group above; upper room in the tower; the cattle-shed history. Also Growse p.256 on the sikhara's square/octagonal lower storey and curvilinear roof, grouping Madan Mohan and Jugal Kishor. Braj Ras (brajrasik.org), 'Shri Yugal Kishor Temple, Vrindavan' (the SEPARATE Nimbarka temple near Jugal Ghat, 300-400 years old, Shri Jugal Bihari palanquin). Panna district government site and Wikipedia 'Hindupat Singh' (deity taken to Panna; temple built 1758-1778). Sunday Guardian, 'Saving Vrindavan' (structurally fragile, uninterpreted). Approx locations (OSM): Kesi Ghat 27.5873 N, 77.6987 E; Jugal Ghat 27.5815 N, 77.6911 E.

temples.name: Shri Govind Dev Ji Mandir (Govindadeva)
temples.material: Ashlar red sandstone throughout, laid in very fine joints ('each and every stone set very neatly'). The 1854 rebuild of the sanctum is rough BRICK, not stone — a deliberate material break at the west end. Later brick/plaster sheds and a modern worship temple stand adjacent.
temples.primaryColour: Deep warm red-to-salmon Bharatpur/Rupbas sandstone. Growse repeatedly stresses 'the natural glow of the red sandstone' and 'the rich glow of the red sand-stone' as the building's defining warmth — the colour IS the architecture here. Weathered surfaces go grey-brown and biologically blackened in shadow; sun-facing faces stay hot orange-red.
temples.accentColour: Patches of white lime-wash on interior walls and pillars up to roughly half their height (applied 1882 by the Jaipur agent, which Growse called 'ruining the architectural effect'; government ordered it undone, but lime ghosting persists). Grey rubble in the rebuilt west wall. Modern cream/ochre plaster on the abutting structures.
temples.approxFootprintM: Greek-cross core approx 30.5 x 30.5 m (nave 100 ft long, breadth across transepts 100 ft — Growse). Walls average 10 ft (3.05 m) thick, so the mass is enormous relative to interior volume. Secondary reports give an outer platform envelope of roughly 60 x 37 m (200 x 120 ft). The moulded plinth was buried under 8 ft (2.4 m) of debris until 1873 — it now stands proud again, which is what gives the base its crispness.
temples.builtYear: 1590 CE (Sanskrit inscription on the NW chapel exterior: 34th year of Akbar's era, founded by Raja Man Singh Deva of Amber). Named craftsmen are on the stone: head of works Kalyan Das, assistant superintendent Manik Chand, ARCHITECT Gobind Das of Delhi, mason Gorakh Das. Aurangzeb-era demolition c.1670. Restored from August 1873 under F.S. Growse.
temples.towerForm: TRUNCATED AND INCOMPLETE — this is the single most important fact for modelling it. The design called for FIVE towers: one over the central crossing plus four over the choir, sacrarium and two side chapels. Today: the sacrarium tower is razed to the ground (only a plinth survives); the two chapel towers were NEVER COMPLETED; the choir (jagmohan) tower survives best but has lost several upper stages — it was restored in the 1870s except the finial and a few top stages. The centre is crowned by a true DOME of 'singularly graceful proportions'. So the silhouette is: one elegant dome, one stubby re-capped spire beside it, and three bare stumps. Growse: the loss of the towers and of the lofty arcaded parapet 'has terribly marred the effect of the exterior and given it a heavy stunted appearance.' Model it squat, broad and beheaded — not as a soaring shikhara.
temples.facade: Walls pierced in TWO STAGES. The lower stage is purely Hindu — trabeate, lintels on straight jambs. The upper stage is a regular TRIFORIUM of Muhammadan (Mughal) character reached by an internal staircase. Critically, the arches are DECORATIVE ONLY, not structural: the spandrels could be knocked out leaving just a lintel on jambs with no loss of stability — and most HAD been knocked out before being re-inserted in the 1870s restoration. So they read as applied cusped/pointed arch-heads filling a post-and-beam frame. External ARCADES run along the north and south sides (pillars, brackets and eaves all renewed in the 1870s). Bold moulded plinth. Richly decorated wall surfaces. A long mutilated Sanskrit tablet sits under one of the west-end niches; a second legible inscription is cut into the NW chapel wall about 10 ft (3 m) above ground.
temples.entrance: THE APPROACH IS THE WHOLE EXPERIENCE. Before 1873 the ONLY access was a narrow winding lane, with houses crowding right up against the temple walls — there was not a single point from which you could see the whole building. Growse demolished houses and cut TWO BROAD APPROACHES: one from the great EASTERN PORTAL (the main axis) and one from the SOUTH TRANSEPT. So the correct game feel is: tight, dark, crowded gali; then you turn and the mass suddenly opens out in front of you. That reveal is designed. The main east entrance leads into a small NARTHEX (porch) 15 ft (4.6 m) deep before the nave. Four corner porches around the central dome were renewed in the 1870s.
temples.roofline: The four arms of the cross are roofed by a POINTED WAGGON VAULT — and this is the rare part: it is built of TRUE RADIATING ARCHES like a Gothic cathedral, not the corbelled/overlapping brackets normal in Hindu work. The whole roof is stone and was thoroughly repaired in the 1870s. The original LOFTY ARCADED PARAPET that crowned the walls is GONE — do not model a parapet. A plain masonry wall (widely believed built by Aurangzeb to desecrate it, possibly Hindu-built for illuminations) once ran along the top of the centre dome; it was demolished as the very first act of the 1873 repairs, so it should NOT be modelled.
temples.compound: Walled courtyard, historically choked with encroaching houses right against the walls; substantially cleared in 1873 and the ground level cut down ~2.4 m to expose the plinth. It sits in a large garden/estate context (the Govind Dev estate sold land to neighbours, e.g. the Seth's temple site). A domed and pillared CHHATRI of very handsome design stands on the platform marking the site of the destroyed sanctum, where it hides the bare rubble wall behind — it was moved there during restoration from its original spot on the south side of the choir. Its inscription reads Sambat 1693, Kartik Badi 5, in the reign of Shah Jahan, erected by Rani Rambhavati, widow of Raja Bhim, son of Rana Amar Singh of Mewar. NOTE: Growse's printed text renders this '1836 A.D.', which is a typo — Sambat 1693 = 1636 CE, and Shah Jahan's reign (1628-58) confirms 1636.
temples.distinguishing: It does not read as a Hindu temple from inside — it reads as a CATHEDRAL. Growse: 'The general effect of the interior is not unlike that produced by Saint Paul's Cathedral in London,' with St Paul's winning on size but Govind Dev winning on the elegance of its central dome and on colour, because the red sandstone supplies 'that relief and warmth of colouring which are so lamentably deficient in its western rival.' A Greek-cross plan, a Hindu elevation, and a Saracenic roof on one building. The other unmistakable thing is the DECAPITATION: a huge, richly carved, obviously unfinished-and-mutilated mass where four of five towers are missing.
temples.interior: Cruciform hall. Nave 100 ft (30.5 m) long, equal transept span, under a pointed stone waggon vault; the crossing opens into the central dome. Growse calls the parts by church names: nave (mandapa/sabha), choir (antarala/jag-mohan), sacrarium (garbha griha), side chapels (mahall). At the WEST end, set between two niches and encased in a RICH CANOPY OF SCULPTURE, a SQUARE-HEADED doorway leads into the choir, a chamber about 20 x 20 ft (6.1 x 6.1 m). Beyond lay the sacrarium flanked by two lateral chapels, each the same 20 ft square and each domed. The SW chapel encloses a subterranean cell called Patal Devi, said by some to be the Goswamis' original shrine of the goddess Vrinda. Lighting is the key: light enters only through the two pierced stages, so you get deep gloom with shafts from the triforium washing red stone — dramatic, high-contrast, cathedral-like. A broken lintel over the north bay of the nave is pinned with three iron bolts (a visible 1870s repair).
temples.deityDescription: DO NOT model Govind Dev here. The original image was moved to Jaipur ahead of Aurangzeb, and the Jaipur Gosain has since been the head of the endowment; the original Govind Dev is in the City Palace complex, Jaipur. What Growse documents in the roughly rebuilt brick sacrarium at Vrindavan (rebuilt c.1854) is an image of KRISHNA AS GIRIDHARI (the mountain-supporter, i.e. lifting Govardhan), with TWO SUBORDINATE FIGURES: one Mahaprabhu (Chaitanya) and one Nityananda. Colour, material and dress of these are NOT documented in the sources I found — do not invent them. Active worship today largely happens in a separate newer temple nearby, not in the historic shell.
temples.confidence: high
temples.sources: F.S. Growse, 'Mathura: A District Memoir' (full text, archive.org/details/mathurdistrict00growrich) — he personally directed the 1873-75 restoration and measured the building; supplemented by en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Govind_Dev_Ji_Temple (thin), uptourism.gov.in, and secondary summaries for the 110 ft / 7-storey original figure. The 110 ft and 'three storeys remain' figures are secondary and less reliable than Growse's plan dimensions; present height ~20 m is MY ESTIMATE from the surviving mass, not a documented figure.

temples.name: Shri Radha Madan Mohan Mandir
temples.material: Red sandstone, including the ghat below, 'all of red stone'. IMPORTANT: the nave was substantially rebuilt in recent times reusing old stone, and WHERE THE OLD STONE RAN SHORT THEY USED BRICK — so the nave is visibly patchwork stone-and-brick while the choir, sanctum tower and south chapel are coherent stone. The separate modern working temple below is later masonry.
temples.primaryColour: Red sandstone, weathered; strong red against the pale river and sky because it stands clear on a bluff. Brick patching in the nave reads as a duller, smaller-module, browner-pink.
temples.accentColour: Grey-white lime mortar in the rebuilt sections; sun-bleached upper surfaces; vegetation staining in joints.
temples.approxFootprintM: Long and narrow, an axial box: nave 57 ft (17.4 m) long + choir 20 ft (6.1 m) square + sanctuary 20 ft (6.1 m) square = roughly 29.5 m total length, and only about 6-8 m wide, PLUS the tower-crowned chapel attached to the south side. So model a slender ~30 x 8 m spine with a bulge on the south flank — not a squat block. The nave's own total height was only about 22 ft (6.7 m).
temples.builtYear: Main temple built by Ram Das 'Kapuri', a Khatri merchant of Multan, from the proceeds of a boat-load of goods sold at Agra, at Sanatana Goswami's instruction; commonly dated c.1580. The south chapel is LATER than the main building, dedicated by one Sri Gunanand (inscription over its east door, given in Bengali then Nagari characters, no date). A door-post on the nave's south side is dated Sambat 1684, but only records a pilgrim's visit. The working temple across the street was built c.1819 by Nandakumar Ghosh, a Bengali Kayastha.
temples.towerForm: NAGARA CURVILINEAR, and the specific geometry is documented: the tower over the SACRARIUM is a PLAIN OCTAGON of curvilinear outline tapering towards the summit — an eight-sided sugarloaf, unornamented. The tower over the CHOIR has had its upper part destroyed (truncated stump). The nave's vaulted roof has ENTIRELY DISAPPEARED — so the nave is roofless or crudely re-covered. The attached south chapel is also tower-crowned, of similar curvilinear character but MUCH more richly enriched and of notably more elegant proportions. Net silhouette: one clean tapering octagonal spire, one richer smaller spire beside it, one broken stump, and an open/ruined nave.
temples.facade: Restrained and massive rather than ornate on the main body. The nave has THREE OPENINGS on either side and a square door at the east end. The south chapel is the decorated element — 'the whole of its exterior surface being covered with sculptured panels', with a single door at its east end carrying the raised (not incised) Sanskrit inscription. Bold moulded plinths, which had been completely buried until Growse cut the ground level down around the chapel in 1875.
temples.entrance: THIS IS THE BEST 'ENTERING' SEQUENCE OF THE FIVE. The temple sits on a high cliff (Dwadashaditya / Duhsasan tila) above Kali-mardan (Kali-dah) Ghat. The old road up was so steep and bad that no cattle could climb it — it was nicknamed the Pasukandan Ghat for exactly that reason. The east door of the nave is a TRAP: immediately outside it the ground drops precipitously 9-10 ft (about 3 m), so you CANNOT enter that way — the only usable entry is FROM THE SIDE. You climb a FLIGHT OF MASONRY STEPS (built 1875 by the municipality for Rs 200) up the ascent from the east, and enter the courtyard through a MASSIVE SQUARE GATEWAY WITH A PYRAMIDAL TOWER, which Growse says 'groups very effectively with the two towers of the temple.' Model the gate so that its pyramid and the two spires compose as one silhouette on the skyline as you climb.
temples.roofline: Curvilinear octagonal spire over the sanctum; broken choir tower; missing nave vault. The pyramidal-towered gateway is part of the roofline composition. Finials/kalasha are not specifically documented in the sources I found — do not invent detail there.
temples.compound: A courtyard on the hilltop reached by the stair and square gateway. A boundary wall was thrown down in 1875 and a NEW APPROACH opened from the east. Buildings that had been built inside the nave and in front of the chapel door were removed. The ghat below, also red stone, was built by the same donor. Sanatana Goswami's bhajan kutir survives in the premises and his samadhi is behind the temple. The temple also owns Ram Tal, a walled garden with a tank at Sunrakh on the Jait road.
temples.distinguishing: THE SILHOUETTE ON THE BLUFF, seen from the river or from Kali-dah Ghat below — a red stone temple standing clear on a cliff above the Yamuna, with the gateway's pyramid and two curvilinear spires stacked against the sky, and a red stone ghat running down to the water. It is the one you see from a distance, not one you stumble into. Second unmistakable thing: the ruined temple is essentially a MUSEUM PIECE — 'not only in ruins, but also from peculiarities of style ill-adapted to modern requirements, they are seldom, if ever, used for religious service', which happens instead in the newer building across the street below.
temples.interior: Axial and simple, not cruciform: nave -> choir -> sanctum in a line, with the south chapel opening off the side. Nave has three openings per side giving cross-light; it is low (about 22 ft / 6.7 m) and now lacks its vault, so it is bright/open where it was once dark. The choir and sanctum are 20 ft (6.1 m) squares under their towers, and are dark. Pillar detail and ceiling carving are not specifically documented for this temple in what I found.
temples.deityDescription: The ORIGINAL Madan Mohan image is NOT here — it is at KARAULI, Rajasthan, where Raja Gopal Singh (r.1725-57) built a new temple for it after obtaining it from his brother-in-law the Raja of Jaipur. A REPLICA was established at Vrindavan in 1748. The altar group as worshipped is THREE figures: MADAN MOHAN (Krishna) in the centre, with RADHA on one side and LALITA (a gopi) on the other. Material, colour and dress are NOT documented in the sources I checked — do not invent. Documented instead is the SEVA RHYTHM, which is good for animating the scene: the god is fed seven times a day; the two principal meals are raj-bhog at midday and sayana at bedtime; the five lighter offerings are mangal arti at dawn, dhup at 9am, sringar at 11am, dhup again at 3pm, and sandhya-arti at dusk.
temples.confidence: high
temples.sources: F.S. Growse, 'Mathura: A District Memoir' (archive.org full text) for all plan dimensions, the cliff/drop, the gateway, the octagonal tower and the 1875 works; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radha_Madan_Mohan_Temple,_Vrindavan for the replica date and the Radha/Lalita group; brajrasik.org for the 1819 lower temple, bhajan kutir and samadhi. CONFLICT: popular sources say '50 feet' or '20 m' high; Growse measured the nave at only ~22 ft. The 50 ft figure most likely describes the temple's crown above the tila, or the tila height above the river. I used ~15 m as a compromise and flag it as uncertain.

temples.name: Shri Radha Vallabh Mandir (old temple / 'Hit Mandir', plus the working temple beside it)
temples.material: Red sandstone — and the sources make a point of this: at that date red sandstone 'was used only for construction of imperial buildings, royal palaces and forts', so using it for a temple was a statement. Stone ceiling panels, stone gable roof. The surviving cella is only a plinth with a later room on top used as a KITCHEN.
temples.primaryColour: Red sandstone, aged to a duller, more lichened red than Govind Dev because it is hemmed in by buildings and gets less sun. The adjoining modern working temple is plastered/painted in light colours (cream/white with colour trim) — the two read as different buildings, which they are.
temples.accentColour: Grey-black biological staining in the shaded lower courses; trees rooted between the roof slabs (Growse warned these would eventually destroy the gable). Bright cloth, tinsel and modern tilework in the active temple.
temples.approxFootprintM: Nave interior 63 x 20 ft (19.2 x 6.1 m) — a long vaulted hall. East facade 34 ft (10.4 m) broad. Walls 10 ft (3.05 m) thick, so external width is roughly 12 m against a 6 m interior. External envelope of the old temple therefore roughly 21 x 12 m, plus the destroyed cella's plinth beyond. Ground plan is 'much the same as' the Harideva temple at Govardhan, but LARGER.
temples.builtYear: 1585 CE, built by Sundardas Bhatnagar, a disciple of Vanachandra (son of Hit Harivansh Mahaprabhu); the sampradaya was founded by Hit Harivansh Mahaprabhu. Growse calls it 'the last example of the early eclectic style' and slightly later than Govind Dev's group.
temples.towerForm: NO TOWER ON THE HALL — and this is the distinctive bit. The outer roof is a STEEP STONE GABLE, which was still perfect in Growse's day. The actual shrine/cella was demolished by Aurangzeb exactly as at Govind Dev, and ONLY THE PLINTH REMAINS, with a later room built on it. So the old temple's profile is a long steep-pitched stone roof with a flat truncated stub where the sanctum spire should be — closer to a stone barn or basilica than to a shikhara temple.
temples.facade: The east facade, 34 ft (10.4 m) broad, is in THREE STAGES with a deliberate stylistic sandwich: upper stage HINDU, middle stage PURELY MUHAMMADAN (arched), lower stage HINDU. Flanks carry a DOUBLE TIER of openings north and south: the LOWER tier has brackets and architraves (trabeate, Hindu); the UPPER tier are Muhammadan ARCHES matching the middle stage of the front. The upper arches open into a narrow gallery with small CLERESTORY WINDOWS looking onto the street. Below, the three CENTRE bays of the colonnade are open doorways; the two END bays are occupied by the staircases up to the gallery. Growse: its 'constructional unity is more striking than its richness of ornamentation' — so keep it architectural and restrained, not encrusted.
temples.entrance: A genuinely good approach for a walkable build: you ASCEND A FLIGHT OF STAIRS and thread a WINDING LANE before you finally arrive at the temple COURTYARD, where the darshan opens in front of you. It sits on a cliff/rise near Gotam Nagar, immediately adjacent to Banke Bihari — a stone's throw away — so the two temples share the same dense lane network and crowd. On the old temple itself, the three central bays of the lower colonnade are the open doorways.
temples.roofline: Steep stone GABLE over the hall (not a vault externally), with carved stone ceiling panels inside, some fallen. Small clerestory windows at gallery level. Truncated cella plinth behind. Trees growing from the roof joints are a real and documented feature.
temples.compound: Wedged into dense urban fabric on a cliff beside Banke Bihari, reached through lanes. The old 1585 temple and the modern working temple stand together — worship happens in the contemporary facilities while the historic shell stands alongside. Courtyard at the top of the stairs.
temples.distinguishing: TWO things. First, architecturally: a temple with a STEEP STONE GABLE ROOF and a two-tier arcaded flank with clerestory windows overlooking the street, plus a headless sanctum — it looks more like a medieval European hall than a North Indian temple, and it has a proper internal triforium gallery you can walk in the thickness of a 3 m wall. Second, ritually, and this is the thing a visitor always remarks on: THERE IS NO RADHA MURTI. A CROWN is placed beside Krishna to signify Radha's presence. The deity is understood as a 'yugal jodi' — Radha and Krishna in one body — and Radha Vallabh Ji's long braid and hair are taken to represent Radha's.
temples.interior: A fine VAULTED HALL, 63 x 20 ft (19.2 x 6.1 m), tall and narrow. Double tier of openings both sides: bracketed-and-architraved below, arched above. An INTERNAL STAIRCASE in the end bays climbs to a narrow upper GALLERY / regular TRIFORIUM running in the wall thickness — the same device as Govind Dev. Carved stone ceiling panels, some fallen. Light comes from the three open doorways at ground level and from the small clerestory windows above, so expect a bright-ends/dark-middle basilica lighting. Beyond the hall, the sanctum is gone — a plinth carrying a room used as a kitchen.
temples.deityDescription: Krishna worshipped as SHRI RADHA VALLABH, 'the consort of Radha'. NO separate Radha image — a CROWN stands for her. Tradition holds the original image was never carved by any sculptor but was divinely given to a devotee named Atmadev. The deity is described as a yugal jodi (Radha and Krishna united in one form), with the long braid/hair read as Radha's. Material, colour, height and daily dress of the murti are NOT documented in the sources I found — do not invent them.
temples.confidence: high
temples.sources: F.S. Growse, 'Mathura: A District Memoir' (archive.org full text) for the facade stages, 63x20 ft hall, double tier, triforium, staircases, gable roof and demolished cella; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radha_Vallabh_Temple,_Vrindavan for 1585, Sundardas Bhatnagar, 10 ft walls, the crown-for-Radha and the Atmadev legend; thegaudiyatreasuresofbengal.com for the stairs/winding lane/courtyard approach and the yugal jodi and braid detail. Architectural confidence high for the OLD temple; LOW for the modern working temple, which I found no reliable dimensioned description of.

temples.name: Shri Banke Bihari Mandir
temples.material: Reported as Rajasthani-style masonry with 'meticulous stonework' and 'carved arched ceilings'. One description notes the ancient tiered structure has ACQUIRED A MORE MODERN LATTICED MARBLE ONE with courtyards and verandas — i.e. an older core progressively refaced and extended in marble. I could NOT find a reliable primary statement of the original stone type. Treat material as: carved sandstone-type masonry core with later marble facing, lattice/jali work and marble flooring.
temples.primaryColour: Not reliably documented. Photographs are consistently described as a light/pale warm facade rather than the deep red of the 16th-century group — plausibly cream, buff or painted render with marble lattice, and heavy applied colour, cloth and gilding around the sanctum. FLAGGING THIS: if you need a colour call, do not copy Govind Dev's red; Banke Bihari reads as a much later, lighter, more ornamental Rajasthani building.
temples.accentColour: Gilded and silvered metalwork at the altar, heavy textiles, marigold garlands, and very heavy crowd-worn polished stone underfoot. No bells anywhere — a visual absence worth modelling.
temples.approxFootprintM: NOT DOCUMENTED in any source I could verify. For context only: the temple sits inside a dense block, and the approved corridor project acquires about 4.74-5 acres around it (roughly 19,000-20,000 sq m) covering about 273 buildings, with an 11,300 sq m ground-floor entrance complex planned — which tells you the temple itself occupies a small fraction of that and is completely hemmed in. Model the temple block at roughly 40 x 40 m with an internal courtyard and treat that as an ESTIMATE, not a source figure.
temples.builtYear: 1862 or 1864 (sources differ; 1864 is the more commonly cited). The deity was moved here from Nidhivan when the temple was built. Associated with Swami Haridas.
temples.towerForm: NOT a curvilinear nagara shikhara and NOT a Dravidian gopuram. Described as a 'tiered structure' in Rajasthani style — i.e. a multi-storey arcaded temple palace-block with a stepped/tiered upper profile, small domed pavilions and chhatri-like crowning elements rather than one dominant spire. Specific finial/kalasha detail is NOT documented; do not invent a big tower.
temples.facade: The one consistently repeated description: RAJASTHANI style, 'adorned with ARCHED WINDOWS and meticulous stonework', with 'carved arched ceilings', and latticed marble with COURTYARDS AND VERANDAS. Read that as tiers of arcaded openings — very likely cusped/multifoil arches on the upper storeys — with jharokha-type projecting balconies and pierced jali screens. I could NOT confirm whether the arches are cusped versus plain pointed, so if precision matters, treat cusped as likely-but-unverified.
temples.entrance: THE APPROACH IS THE ICONIC PART AND IT IS EXTREMELY WELL ATTESTED. You cannot drive there. Vehicles stop well short; the last stretch is on foot or by rickshaw through NARROW LANES packed with shops selling flowers, sweets and religious goods — a continuous bazaar tunnel, loud, crowded, often shoulder-to-shoulder. The temple has MULTIPLE NUMBERED GATES (Gate No. 1, Gate No. 2 etc.); Gate No. 2 is a common entry. At the gate you surrender SHOES, BELT AND BAGS to a stand in exchange for a token. Photography inside is prohibited. For a GTA-style build this is the money sequence: compressed noisy bazaar -> gate and shoe-stand -> release into the courtyard.
temples.roofline: Tiered, with verandas and latticed marble screens; small domed/chhatri elements consistent with Rajasthani work. NOT documented in detail — avoid committing to a specific finial or flag arrangement.
temples.compound: A walled temple block with internal COURTYARD and verandas, fully enclosed by the dense town — about 273 buildings sit within the currently proposed acquisition footprint around it. The courtyard fills to a crush; the planned corridor is designed for 10,000 devotees at a time, which tells you the current capacity is the binding constraint. Radha Vallabh temple is 'a stone's throw away' — the two share the same lane network.
temples.distinguishing: THE CURTAIN. Unlike anywhere else, darshan is not continuous: a curtain is drawn shut and reopened every few minutes (commonly stated as every one to five minutes), because Bihari Ji's gaze is held to be so overpowering that uninterrupted viewing is dangerous. Every few minutes the entire crowd surges and roars. Second: THERE ARE NO BELLS — none are hung anywhere in the premises, and no early-morning arti is performed (mangala arti happens only once a year, on Janmashtami). Third: the lotus feet are normally COVERED and can be seen only on AKSHAYA TRITIYA, one day a year; the flute is held only on SHARAD PURNIMA, when he also wears a special mukut. During Shravan he is placed on a swing for a day.
temples.interior: A courtyard-and-veranda plan rather than a long axial hall: you emerge from the gate into an open courtyard facing the sanctum across it, with arcaded verandas and latticed marble around. Carved arched ceilings. The sanctum is raised and framed by an ornamented altar with the curtain across it. Lighting is the thing to get right: the courtyard is open and bright, the shrine recess is dark and intensely lit on the deity, and the curtain cycle means the light source at the focal point switches on and off every few minutes. Specific pillar orders and altar materials are NOT reliably documented.
temples.deityDescription: WELL DOCUMENTED AND DISTINCTIVE. A BLACK STONE (frequently described as black marble) murti, held to be SWAYAMBHU (self-manifested), not sculptor-made. TRIBHANGA posture — body bent at three points: neck, waist and knee. Worshipped and treated as a small CHILD, with the belief that the vigraha feels soft like human skin. Richly dressed daily in fresh clothes and ornaments, with the tradition that an outfit is not simply repeated identically, so the appearance changes day to day. The FLUTE is held only on Sharad Purnima (with a special crown that day). The LOTUS FEET are kept covered and revealed only on Akshaya Tritiya. Exact height of the murti is not reliably documented in what I found; do not state one.
temples.confidence: medium
temples.sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banke_Bihari_Temple (tribhanga, child-form, curtain, no bells, no mangala arti except Janmashtami, flute on Sharad Purnima, swing in Shravan); tourmyindia.com and srimandir.com (1864, Rajasthani style, arched windows, carved arched ceilings); tirthayatra.org (black stone, swayambhu, Akshaya Tritiya charan darshan, soft-to-touch belief); Tripadvisor/traveller descriptions via search (narrow bazaar lanes, numbered gates, shoe/belt/bag token, no photography, 'latticed marble with courtyards and verandas'); swarajyamag.com / thedailyjagran.com / organiser.org (corridor: 4.74-5 acres, ~273 buildings, 11,300 sq m entrance complex, 10,000 capacity, Rs 262-500 crore). CONFIDENCE IS MEDIUM ONLY: ritual and approach are very well attested, but I found NO trustworthy dimensioned or material survey of the building. Do not treat my height/footprint numbers as sourced.

temples.name: Shri Gopishwar Mahadev Mandir
temples.material: NOT DOCUMENTED in any source I could verify. I found no statement of stone type, render or colour from a survey, trust or ASI record. Do not commit to red sandstone or marble on my authority.
temples.primaryColour: NOT DOCUMENTED. I am explicitly declining to guess. If you must build it, treat it as a modest lime-washed/rendered masonry courtyard shrine of no fixed colour and revise from photographs.
temples.accentColour: NOT DOCUMENTED, except that the focal object is the linga itself under heavy applied decoration (see deity).
temples.approxFootprintM: NOT DOCUMENTED. The only structural fact I could verify is that it has a LARGE OPEN COURTYARD, which implies a compound noticeably wider than the shrine. My 10 m height figure is an ESTIMATE for a single-storey courtyard shrine, not a source figure.
temples.builtYear: Traditionally ascribed to VAJRANABHA, great-grandson of Krishna — i.e. a legendary/mythic foundation date, not a historical one. No historical construction date is documented. Note that F.S. Growse's exhaustive 1880s survey lists 'Gopesvar Mahadeva' ONLY as the name of a mahalla (a neighbourhood ward) of Vrindavan and gives NO architectural description at all — which is itself informative: it was not, in his time, a monument of architectural note.
temples.towerForm: NOT DOCUMENTED. Style is described only as 'a mix of Rajasthani and Nagar styles'. That phrasing is from a popular temple site, not a survey, and is too vague to model from. Do not build a specific shikhara on this basis.
temples.facade: NOT DOCUMENTED. No source I found describes arches, jali, columns, carved bands or balconies for this temple.
temples.entrance: Not documented in detail. What IS documented and useful: it stands near VAMSHI VAT, on the bank of the Yamuna, and the complex contains a large open courtyard used for ritual and prayer, with a prominent PEEPAL TREE regarded as a Kalpavriksha (wish-fulfilling tree). So the entering sequence is: river/Vamsivat side of town -> into an open courtyard dominated by a sacred peepal -> shrine facing it. That courtyard-plus-tree relationship is the one spatial fact worth building.
temples.roofline: NOT DOCUMENTED.
temples.compound: Documented: a LARGE OPEN COURTYARD for rituals and prayer, containing a venerated Peepal tree. Relative size versus the shrine is not stated, but 'large open courtyard' plus a single-cell Shiva shrine implies the COURTYARD dominates and the shrine is small — the inverse of Govind Dev.
temples.distinguishing: UNAMBIGUOUSLY THE GOPI-VESH, and it is a time-of-day mechanic, which is perfect for a walkable build. The SAME Shiva linga is presented two completely different ways in one day. By DAY (roughly 6-10am; temple open from about 5am-12pm, aarti ~7:30-8:30am) it is worshipped as a plain Shiva linga, the symbol of male power. By EVENING (roughly 5-9pm; open about 4:30-9:30pm, aarti ~7:30-8:30pm) the linga is DRESSED AS A GOPI with full shringar, because Shiva took gopi form to be admitted to the Ras Lila. The theology is explicitly the meeting of masculine and feminine. So: same geometry, two entirely different material/decor states, switched at dusk. That, plus the Kalpavriksha peepal in the courtyard, is what makes it recognisable.
temples.interior: NOT DOCUMENTED. No source I found describes the hall type, pillars, sanctum framing or lighting. The only safe statement is that the focus is a Shiva linga in a sanctum opening onto the courtyard.
temples.deityDescription: A SHIVA LINGA — Shiva as Gopeshwar, 'lord of the gopis'. Documented: worshipped as a bare linga in the morning, and 'adorned with beautiful gopi decorations' / dressed as a gopi with special shringar in the evening for the Ras Lila. Beyond that, THE SPECIFICS ARE NOT DOCUMENTED in the sources I checked: I could not verify the linga's size, stone colour, or the exact components of the gopi dress (saree colour, crown, nose-ring, jewellery). Several popular pages assert such details without sourcing. DO NOT MODEL SPECIFIC ORNAMENTS ON MY AUTHORITY — build the two-state mechanic and get the dress detail from photographs or from the temple directly.
temples.confidence: low
temples.sources: srimandir.com (Vajranabha attribution, 'mix of Rajasthani and Nagar styles', large open courtyard, peepal/Kalpavriksha, darshan timings); holidify.com and thegaudiyatreasuresofbengal.com (gopi-vesh morning/evening split, location near Vamshi Vat on the Yamuna); F.S. Growse, 'Mathura: A District Memoir' — NEGATIVE EVIDENCE, lists Gopesvar Mahadeva only as a mahalla name with no architectural description; architexturez.net holds photographs of the temple but NO descriptive text. THIS IS THE WEAKEST-DOCUMENTED OF THE FIVE BY A LARGE MARGIN. The ritual is well attested; the building is essentially undocumented in text. Send someone with a camera, or work from photographs, before modelling it in detail.

temples.name: Shri Rangaji Mandir (Sri Ranganath / Rangji Mandir), Goda Vihar, Vrindavan
temples.material: Load-bearing masonry. The gopurams are brick/rubble cores finished in lime plaster with modelled stucco figure sculpture (standard Dravidian practice) and painted. The two ceremonial outer gates are carved dressed sandstone in the Jaipur/'Mathura' idiom. Long colonnades with square stone piers. The flagstaff is gilded copper sheet over a core. Built 1845-1851 by Seths Gobind Das and Radha Krishan, to plans by Swami Rangacharya, with craftsmen brought from Srirangam; cost Rs 45 lakh.
temples.primaryColour: NOT DOCUMENTED in the text sources I could verify. Do NOT model this as a red-sandstone temple. Dravidian stucco gopurams of this type are lime-white/cream overall with polychrome painted figure tiers (repainted periodically, so the palette has changed over time); the stone gates and colonnades read pale buff/ochre sandstone. Treat the white-plus-polychrome reading as an informed inference, not a citation.
temples.accentColour: Gold (gilded 50-60 ft dhwaja/Garuda stambha, kalashas); polychrome reds, blues, yellows and greens on the gopuram figure sculpture; deep shadow in the corridors.
temples.approxFootprintM: Outer walls 773 ft x 440 ft = approx. 236 m x 134 m (about 3.2 hectares) - Growse, 1883, measured. Five concentric rectangular prakara (enclosure) walls inside that. The built temple occupies only a modest fraction; most of the walled area is open ground, tank and garden.
temples.builtYear: Begun 1845, completed 1851
temples.towerForm: Dravidian gopurams - tiered, inward-battering towers, each tier a row of pilastered niches and stucco figures, capped by a barrel-vaulted shala roof carrying a row of kalashas. West gopuram seven storeys, east gopuram five storeys; secondary sources describe eight gopurams in all across the enclosures. The sanctum itself carries a low vimana, NOT a north-Indian curvilinear shikhara.
temples.facade: Two distinct architectural languages in one compound. (a) Dravidian: gopuram tiers of pilastered niches, kudu (horseshoe-arch) motifs and dense figure sculpture - Growse calls it 'a profusion of coarse sculpture'. (b) North Indian: the two outer stone gates are Jaipur-style carved work with cusped/multifoil arches, fine pierced jali ('elegance of its reticulated tracery' - Growse), bracketed chhajja eaves and chhatris. (c) The prakara corridors are long pillared colonnades on square/lathe-turned piers; one visitor account calls the colonnade 'distinctly Italian' in feel because of its length and regularity.
temples.entrance: The set piece: at the principal (western) entrance a carved stone pavilion 93 ft (28.3 m) high in the local north-Indian style stands in FRONT of the Dravidian gopura, which rises immediately behind it - a Rajput gate and a Tamil tower stacked one behind the other on the same axis. Growse contrasts the pavilion's 'graceful outlines' against the 'heavy and misshapen masses of the Madras Gopura'. Today the east gate off Rangji Mandir Road is the working entrance. Low steps, shoe deposit, camera restriction, then straight into a long shaded colonnade.
temples.roofline: Each gopuram tier capped by a barrel-vaulted shala with a ridge row of kalashas; gilded finials at the apex. The stone gates carry chhatris and carved parapets. On the sanctum axis stands the dhwaja/Garuda stambha - Growse measured it at 60 ft (18.3 m) above ground with a further 24 ft buried, gilt copper, cost Rs 10,000; the temple trust and UP Tourism both say 50 ft gold-plated. Use 15-18 m and note the conflict.
temples.compound: Fully walled rectangle approx. 236 x 134 m, five concentric prakaras. Inside the outer enclosure, between the two gopurams, a large pushkarini (masonry bathing tank); opposite it a garden with stone fountains; a Barahdwari pavilion and a Hanuman shrine between garden and east gopuram; a Vahan Ghar housing the processional vehicles; a Sheesh Mahal used at the swing festival; a yagyashala. A detached shed by the entrance holds the rath - an enormous multi-stage wooden tower (trust says approx. 50 ft) with large effigies at the corners, brought out once a year in Chait for Brahmotsav and hauled 690 yards along the road to the garden pavilion. Compound dwarfs the temple: this is a precinct, not a building.
temples.distinguishing: The only Dravidian temple in Braj, and the only place in India where a South Indian gopuram rises directly behind a Rajput carved-stone gate. Plus the gilded flagstaff and the vast quiet walled garden-and-tank precinct - you step off a crowded Vrindavan street and are suddenly in a huge, empty, sunlit rectangle that feels like Tamil Nadu.
temples.interior: Concentric walled courts linked by long, low, colonnaded corridors - pillared, dim, with light dropping in from open courtyards at the ends. A garuda mandapa on the sanctum axis; the sanctum reached through a small doorway with the gilded dhwaja stambha standing directly in front. Growse also records a gallery of mythological tableaux with electrically operated dolls (Entwistle repeats this). Lighting model: hard sun in the open courts, deep shade under the colonnades, oil-lamp/electric warm light at the sanctum.
temples.deityDescription: UNRESOLVED - flag this to the artist. The temple trust's own site and Braj Ras name the deity Sri Goda-Rangamannar, a divine couple: Krishna standing as a bridegroom with a walking stick in his hand, in the South Indian marriage convention, with Andal (Goda Devi) to his right and Garuda to his left. Many tourist sites instead describe a reclining Ranganatha on the coils of Sesha, as at Srirangam. These are incompatible. The trust's description should be preferred, but do not model the sanctum image without a photographic reference. The utsava (processional) murti is documented by Growse as being made of ashtadhatu, the eight metals, and rides the rath at Brahmotsav flanked by Brahmans with chauris.
temples.confidence: high on plan, dimensions, gates, flagstaff, rath and history (Growse 1883 is an eyewitness measured account, corroborated by the temple trust); medium on gopuram storey counts and total heights; low on colour; low on the sanctum image.
temples.sources: F. S. Growse, 'Mathura: A District Memoir' (1883), ch. IX 'Brinda-ban and its Temples' / 'The Seth's Temple', full text at archive.org/stream/mathurdistrict00growrich; srirangjimandir.org (temple trust, History & Architecture page); uptourism.gov.in Rangaji Temple page; brajrasik.org 'Shri Rangji Mandir, Vrindavan'; A. W. Entwistle, 'Braj: Centre of Krishna Pilgrimage', full text at archive.org; vrindavantoday.in 'Splendid architecture of Shri Rangnath temple'.

temples.name: Prem Mandir, Raman Reti / Bhaktivedanta Swami Marg, Vrindavan
temples.material: White Italian Carrara marble throughout - roughly 30,000 tonnes of it - on a 20 ft deep granite foundation; walls stated as 3.25 ft of solid marble. Semi-precious stone inlay in floors and walls. Sandalwood sanctum doors with inlaid stone lettering. Built Jan 2001 to Feb 2012, approx. 1,000 artisans, Rs 150 crore, founded by Jagadguru Shri Kripalu Ji Maharaj.
temples.primaryColour: Brilliant white, and uniformly so - there is no contrasting stone. This is the key material read: a single-material, single-colour, heavily undercut carved mass. Cast strong ambient occlusion in the carving or it will look flat.
temples.accentColour: Coloured semi-precious stone inlay (floral vines, flowers, buds) in floors and walls; 17 gold-coloured kalashas; green lawns all round. At night the whole marble body is washed by colour-changing LED floodlight cycling through blue, pink, green and amber - the building visibly changes colour every few seconds, and the musical fountain jets (25-30 ft) are lit to match.
temples.approxFootprintM: Temple body approx. 37 x 35 m (122 ft x 115 ft). Raised platform approx. 58 x 39 m (190 ft x 128 ft). A 40 ft (12 m) wide parikrama runs round the platform. Campus 22 hectares / 55 acres. Note the two size figures in circulation are the building and the plinth respectively, not a contradiction.
temples.builtYear: Foundation 14 Jan 2001; inaugurated 15-17 Feb 2012
temples.towerForm: Nagara, in a Rajasthani/Gujarati/Somnath idiom - a cluster of curvilinear shikhara and dome forms rather than one spire. Nine carved domes, crowned by 17 gold-coloured kalashas, with the flag taking total height to 125 ft.
temples.facade: Every surface carved. 84 panels of Radha-Krishna leelas on the outer walls; 150 carved pillars; cusped and multifoil arches; carved brackets, small balconies and jali screens; continuous bands of floral scroll. The silhouette is stepped and bristling rather than smooth. There are no flat wall planes at eye level.
temples.entrance: The arrival sequence is the point. Off Raman Reti road through a gated, guarded forecourt; shoe deposit and a security/metal-detector line; then a long paved walk across manicured lawns with the whole white mass in front of you the entire way (unlike the old-town temples, you see this one from far off); then a broad flight of steps onto the raised marble platform; then a carved doorway into the ground-floor hall. Evening is the intended arrival - darshan, dusk, colour-wash, fountain show.
temples.roofline: Nine domes/shikharas, 17 gilded kalashas, carved parapets, small chhatris and a flag at the apex.
temples.compound: 55-acre walled campus, gardens and fountains, the temple standing free in the middle of lawns. Beside it a separate pillar-less dome-shaped Satsang Hall of 6,800 sq m (73,000 sq ft) seating 25,000. In the gardens, life-size walk-up dioramas of four leelas: Govardhan leela as a built artificial hill, Kaliya Naag leela set in a water tank, Jhulan leela (swing) and Raas leela. Plus the musical fountain with a 30-minute evening show (roughly 19:00-19:30 winter, 19:30-20:00 summer). Entry free.
temples.distinguishing: A white marble wedding cake standing alone in a park, floodlit at night in cycling colours, with a walk-through Govardhan hill and a fountain show. It is the only temple in Braj that is built and operated like an attraction - wide, open, legible, photographed from a distance.
temples.interior: Two levels, each a pillared hall wrapped round a central sanctum, with 150 carved pillars (carved with Kinkari and Manjari sakhis in service). Semi-precious stone inlay underfoot and on the walls; a 20 ft chandelier over the sanctum; sandalwood sanctum doors. The 40 ft parikrama on the platform carries 80 three-dimensional panels telling Krishna's pastimes from the Bhagavata in sequence. Interior walls also carry Kripalu Ji Maharaj's devotional verse, engraved.
temples.deityDescription: Ground floor: Radha Krishna, flanked by the eight Mahasakhis, with statues of Jagadguru Kripalu Ji Maharaj and Sukhdev Paramhans and wall depictions of Radha-Krishna pastimes. First floor: Sita Ram with Hanuman, with scenes from Chaitanya Mahaprabhu's life and statues of the four previous Jagadgurus. (Wikipedia words the levels as Radha Krishna on the first level and Sita Ram on the second - same arrangement, different counting convention.) The daily dress and ornament of the deities is NOT documented in any source I could verify; they are changed regularly in silk poshak and jewellery, so do not model a fixed costume as canonical.
temples.confidence: high on material, dimensions, dates, layout, leela dioramas and the light show (temple trust site plus Wikipedia plus consistent secondary accounts); medium on the 150-pillar / 9-dome / 17-kalash / 30,000-tonne counts, which trace to a single detailed account; low on deity dress.
temples.sources: premmandir.org.in 'The Architecture'; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prem_Mandir,_Vrindavan; ghumakkar.com 'Prem Mandir - Vrindavan: Unique combination of Devotion, Art and Grandeur' (detailed measured account: 125 x 122 x 115 ft, 150 pillars, 9 domes, 17 kalash, 30,000 t marble, 40 ft parikrama with 80 panels, 20 ft chandelier); multiple visitor guides for the fountain and LED show timings.

temples.name: Sri Sri Krishna Balaram Mandir (ISKCON Vrindavan), Raman Reti, Bhaktivedanta Swami Marg
temples.material: White marble throughout - carved walls, arcades, domes, staircases and archways. The courtyard floor is black-and-white chequered marble. Gold-plated flagstaffs and kalashas. Giant timber entrance doors. (The specific marble quarry is not documented in the sources I found; do not assert Makrana.) Deities installed by A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada on Ram Navami, 20 April 1975; complex completed 1977; Prabhupada oversaw the design personally.
temples.primaryColour: White marble, with a strong black-and-white chequerboard on the sunken courtyard floor - that chequer is the single most recognisable surface on the site.
temples.accentColour: Gold on flagstaffs, kalashas and altar surrounds; saffron/orange flags; brightly coloured deity dress and flower garlands against the white; warm chandelier light on the altars.
temples.approxFootprintM: NOT DOCUMENTED. The temple is a single large hall raised on a plinth above a sunken courtyard, within a walled campus that also holds the samadhi mandir and museum, a Gurukula, a guest house, Govinda's restaurant, a goshala, book stalls, a bakery, Prabhupada's rear quarters and a Tulsi garden used for parikrama. Do not publish a footprint figure as fact.
temples.builtYear: Deities installed 20 April 1975; complex completed 1977; Prabhupada's samadhi begun c. 1980, opened early 1980s
