temples.towerForm: Three white marble curvilinear nagara shikharas, one over each of the three altars, crowned with gilded kalashas and gold-plated flagstaffs. Note: the three-shikhara reading is consistent with the three-altar plan and with secondary descriptions of 'carved walls and domes', but no source I found states the count explicitly - verify against a photograph before finalising the silhouette.
temples.facade: White marble arcades of cusped arches; carved marble balconies and pierced jali; a winding staircase; a brilliant white marble archway at the entrance leading to the huge wooden doors.
temples.entrance: Off Bhaktivedanta Swami Marg in Raman Reti. Through the campus gate into a forecourt - and the first thing you meet is NOT the temple but Prabhupada's samadhi mandir: white marble, central spire 70 ft (21 m), white marble elephants, lions, swans and peacocks on the facade, curving 'peacock' staircases up to a painting gallery, flanked by waterfalls, fountains and flower canopies, with a diorama museum. Only then, under the white marble archway and through the giant wooden doors, into the sunken chequered courtyard; then up the steps to the temple room. That two-stage arrival - memorial first, temple second - is exactly what makes the entry feel real.
temples.roofline: Three shikharas with gilded kalashas and gold-plated flagstaffs; parapets with small finials; the samadhi's 70 ft spire dominating the forecourt.
temples.compound: Walled campus. IMPORTANT for a rebuild: many of the original 1975 buildings, including the Gurukula complex, have been declared structurally unsafe by engineers and a new Krishna Balaram Cultural Centre has been under construction with a target tied to the mandir's 2025 fiftieth anniversary. The campus you model will differ depending on the year you pick.
temples.distinguishing: The sunken black-and-white chequerboard courtyard, open to the sky, ringed by white marble arcades, with a living tamal tree growing in it - and 24-hour kirtan with kartals, mridanga and harmonium audible from the street outside. Nothing else in Vrindavan has that courtyard.
temples.interior: One large marble temple room facing three altars set in a row along one wall - not a nave-and-aisle plan but an open hall for kirtan and dancing. Altars framed by carved marble arches, fitted with grilles and curtains that open and close for darshan, backed with mirrors and lit by chandeliers. Polished marble floor. Daylight arrives indirectly off the open courtyard, so the hall is bright but shadowless while the altars are the warm focal points.
temples.deityDescription: Three altars, all installed 20 April 1975. CENTRE: Krishna and Balarama, standing as brothers. RIGHT: Radha-Shyamasundar, with the gopis Lalita and Vishakha - Prabhupada personally posed for Radharani's stance, so her pose differs from the usual convention. LEFT: Gaura-Nitai (Chaitanya Mahaprabhu and Nityananda), together with murtis of Prabhupada himself and his guru Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati. The deities are dressed daily in elaborate silk with jewellery and fresh flower garlands; the colours change every day, so no fixed outfit should be treated as canonical. Deity heights and materials are NOT documented in the sources I found.
temples.confidence: medium-high on altar arrangement, courtyard, samadhi and dates (Wikipedia, ISKCON's own Back to Godhead, and consistent devotee accounts); medium on the shikhara count and facade detail; low on all measurements of the temple building itself - only the samadhi's 70 ft spire is documented.
temples.sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISKCON_Temple,_Vrindavan; back2godhead.com 'Srila Prabhupada Shrine (Samadhi) Under Way in Vrindavan' (Back to Godhead, Sept 1980 - source of the 70 ft spire, marble elephants/lions/swans/peacocks, curving staircases, waterfalls, museum); thegaudiyatreasuresofbengal.com 'Iskcon Vrindavan: Sri Krishna Balaram Mandir' (sunken chequered courtyard, tamal tree, marble archway and giant wooden doors, 24-hour kirtan, 30 departments); vrajvrindavan.com altar-by-altar listing; iskconvrindavan.com new-construction page (1975 buildings unsafe).

temples.name: Vrindavan Chandrodaya Mandir, Bhaktivedanta Swami Marg / Chhatikara side, Vrindavan
temples.material: Reinforced concrete structural system - structural design by the Department of Civil Engineering, IIT, with Sanrachna Consultants (New Delhi); architecture by InGenious Studio Pvt Ltd; developed by ISKCON Bangalore. Engineered for Richter 8.0 and 170 km/h winds; approx. 511 pillars; total mass approx. 500,000 tonnes; foundation proportionally deeper than the Burj Khalifa's. Final cladding material is NOT documented - renders show a pale stone-toned skin; the structure on site today is grey concrete.
temples.primaryColour: Today: bare grey concrete and steel. As rendered: pale cream/sandstone-toned tiered tower. Do not treat the render colour as documented fact.
temples.accentColour: None documented.
temples.approxFootprintM: Tower footprint approx. 5 acres (about 2 hectares, roughly a 140 x 140 m field); built-up area 50,000 sq m (540,000 sq ft). Temple complex 26 acres within a 260-hectare (642-acre) land holding, plus 4.9 hectares (12 acres) of parking and a helipad.
temples.builtYear: Foundation stone 16 March 2014; still unfinished; current stated completion December 2028 after missed targets in 2019, 2022, 2024, 2025 and 2026
temples.towerForm: A nagara shikhara scaled up to a skyscraper. In plan a square with graduated projections at the middle of each side producing a cruciform; in elevation the shikhara inclines inwards on a convex curve with strong vertical emphasis, stepped into tiers - repeatedly described as rocket-ship-like or pyramid-like. Planned as the tallest religious monument in the world. Floor count is given as 70 in the architectural sources and 75 on Wikipedia; a popular '166 floors' claim is not consistent with either and should be discarded.
temples.facade: Vertical pilaster bands and tiered setbacks, per the renders. A capsule elevator carries visitors to a top-floor viewing gallery named 'Braj Mandal Darshan'. Detailed facade articulation is not documented in text.
temples.entrance: Vehicle approach on the new side of Vrindavan (Bhaktivedanta Swami Marg / Chhatikara), open flat land rather than old-town lanes - you drive in, you do not walk in through a gali.
temples.roofline: A single crowning shikhara with kalasha, per the published renders. Unbuilt.
temples.compound: Planned: 26-acre complex with four temples, twelve recreated forests of Braj, a heritage museum, boating zone, Radha-Krishna recreational park, rides, a Vedic-themed park with light and sound, a 10,000-capacity assembly, helipad and parking. Currently built: a working temple with deities running a full ISKCON aarti cycle, a goshala, and event facilities - plus the unfinished structure and cranes.
temples.distinguishing: CRITICAL FOR THE ARTIST: the 700 ft tower does not exist. As of 2026 what stands on site is a large unfinished concrete structure amid construction plant, with a functioning small temple and goshala operating beside it. If you model the render, you are modelling something nobody has ever seen. If you model the site, you are modelling a building site with a live temple in it. Decide which, and say which.
temples.interior: Not built. No documented interior.
temples.deityDescription: Dedicated to Radha Krishna. The operational temple on site runs the standard ISKCON worship cycle. The final sanctum deities of the tower are not documented.
temples.confidence: medium on the design intent, dimensions, engineering and programme (architect and engineer credits, Skyscraper Center, Wikipedia, ISKCON Bangalore); high on the fact that the tower is unbuilt; low on everything about its finished appearance.
temples.sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vrindavan_Chandrodaya_Mandir; designingbuildings.co.uk wiki entry (cruciform plan, convex-curve shikhara, vertical emphasis, InGenious Studio, capsule elevator, 12 forests); skyscrapercenter.com building 27816; architizer.com InGenious Studio project page; organiser.org 19 Nov 2024 (511 pillars, 500,000 t, seismic and wind design); vcm.org.in; vrindavantoursandpackages.com Chandrodaya status guide (explicit statement that the tower is not built and what exists today).

temples.name: Shahji Mandir (official name Lalit Nikunj), near Nidhivan, Vrindavan
temples.material: White marble, described throughout as Italian marble; the spiral columns are each cut from a single block. Growse, who saw it new, records it as 'constructed of the most costly materials' and 'fronted with a colonnade of spiral marble pillars, each shaft being of a single piece'. Built 1876 by the Lucknow jeweller brothers Shah Kundan Lal and Shah Phundan Lal; Growse gives the cost as ten lakh rupees.
temples.primaryColour: White marble outside. Inside, the Basanti Kamra is a yellow room - 'Basanti' is spring yellow - with painted ceilings and walls.
temples.accentColour: Yellow (Basanti Kamra decor); the glitter and refraction of Belgian glass chandeliers; multicoloured Raas-leela paintings on ceiling and walls; water from the central fountain.
temples.approxFootprintM: NOT DOCUMENTED. It is a courtyard temple wedged into a dense lane near Nidhivan, with a walled courtyard and the Basanti Kamra at its east end. Small by comparison with Rangaji or Prem Mandir - the whole thing reads as a mansion facade addressing a private courtyard, not a precinct.
temples.towerForm: NOT a shikhara temple at all - this is the key modelling decision. Flat-roofed and terraced, with a classical pediment over the colonnade. Growse describes 'its uncouth pediment, flanked by sprawling monsters'. The twelve columns are described as supporting the terraces above. Lucknavi-European, not Hindu-temple, massing.
temples.facade: A colonnade of twelve white marble spiral (twisted / barley-sugar / Solomonic) columns, each a single shaft 15 ft (4.6 m) tall and 35 inches (about 0.89 m) in diameter. Above them a pediment flanked by sculpted sprawling monsters, and across the front a row of life-size female figures - Growse's eyewitness description, and the reason he compared the whole facade to 'a disreputable London casino'. Growse also thought the shafts 'rather too attenuated' but 'unquestionably elegant'. The style is repeatedly described as a blend of Mughal, European/Greek and Hindu.
temples.entrance: Reached through a narrow gali near Nidhivan - you cannot see the temple until you are at its gate. The principal entrance to the courtyard is, in Growse's words, 'in a grandiose way, decidedly effective'. From the courtyard, steps up to the colonnaded porch under the twelve columns.
temples.roofline: Flat terrace with parapet/balustrade plus the pediment. No curvilinear tower, no kalasha-crowned shikhara. Getting this right is what separates a correct Shahji from a generic Vrindavan temple.
temples.compound: A walled courtyard hemmed in by houses. The Basanti Kamra (Durbar hall) occupies the east end of the courtyard. The samadhi of Shri Lalit Kishori stands near the temple.
temples.distinguishing: The twelve twisted marble columns - locals call it Tedhe Khambe Wala Mandir, 'the temple of the crooked pillars'. A Lucknow nawabi palace facade with a European pediment and life-size marble women, standing in a Vrindavan lane. There is nothing else like it in Braj.
temples.interior: The Basanti Kamra, the yellow Durbar hall, is the interior worth building: Belgian glass chandeliers, painted ceiling and interior walls covered with Raas-leela and Krishna-life scenes, and fountains in the central part of the hall. It is opened to the public only around Basant Panchami (sources say twice a year). The sanctum proper is small; the deities are small. Lighting: dim, chandelier-lit, refracted - the opposite of Prem Mandir's flood-lit white.
temples.deityDescription: Radha and Krishna, known as 'Chhote Radha Raman' - 'little Radha-Raman' - specifically because the murtis are small. The establishment's own name is Lalit Nikunj, with Lalit Kishori and Lalit Mohini named as the sevya thakur. Sources say only that they are richly adorned; no documented fixed form, colour or ornament. Do not invent one. NOTE a naming trap: Growse (1883) refers to this temple as 'the temple of Radha Raman ... founded by Sah Kundan Lal of Lakhnau'. That is THIS temple, not the separate and much older Gaudiya Radha Raman temple of Gopal Bhatta Goswami.
temples.confidence: high on the columns, facade sculpture, pediment, Basanti Kamra, founders, date and cost - Growse saw the building when it was almost new, and modern accounts agree with him a century and a half later; low on overall height, storeys and footprint, none of which is documented. The 11 m height is my inference from the 15 ft columns plus entablature and terrace, not a citation.
temples.sources: F. S. Growse, 'Mathura: A District Memoir' (1883) - eyewitness description of Sah Kundan Lal's temple, spiral marble monolithic pillars, pediment with sprawling monsters, life-size female figures, ten lakh cost; astroved.com Shahji Temple page (12 spiral columns, 15 ft high, 35 in diameter); brajrasik.org 'Shahji temple - Tede Khambe wala Vrindavan' (Lalit Nikunj, Basanti Kamra at east end of courtyard, chandeliers, fountains, Basant Panchami opening, Lalit Kishori samadhi); vrindavandarshanguide.com (12 columns each from one marble piece, supporting the terraces); A. W. Entwistle, 'Braj', which quotes Growse's casino comparison.

temples.name: Nidhivan (Nidhuvan), Gopinath Bagh, Vrindavan
temples.material: Not a monument — a walled sacred grove. Built fabric is minor and secondary: a low perimeter wall of lime-plastered/whitewashed brick with a painted dado, stone-flag and brick-paved paths, and inside it the Rang Mahal, a small shrine reported as marble (white) with a marble-faced chamber. Other structures (Bansi Chor Radharani temple, Swami Haridas shrine/samadhi, Banke Bihari prakatya sthal) are small plastered-masonry shrines, not dressed-stone temples. Materials for individual shrines are NOT documented in any authoritative source.
temples.primaryColour: Overwhelmingly the dark olive-green-to-black of the grove: the trees are the architecture. Built elements read as chalky white / cream lime-wash with saffron and red-ochre trim; Rang Mahal reads white/ivory.
temples.accentColour: Saffron and vermilion (flags, tilak marks, cloth), marigold orange and tulsi green from offerings, bright synthetic-red and gold of the Rang Mahal's dressed bed, blue-and-white painted signage.
temples.approxFootprintM: Published figure: about 12 acres (~48,000 m², i.e. very roughly a 220 m × 220 m walled block) at Gopinath Bagh. Treat as approximate — it comes from tourism copy, not a survey. The Rang Mahal itself is small, of the order of 6–10 m square. Grove canopy is LOW: the trees are stunted and bent, roughly 3–5 m, not forest-scale.
temples.builtYear: The grove is treated as immemorial. The Banke Bihari murti was worshipped here by Swami Haridas (16th c.) and installed in the Rang Mahal, where tradition says it stayed 266 years before moving to the Banke Bihari temple built c. 1862–64. Present built fabric is late and repeatedly renewed; no construction date is documented.
temples.towerForm: Effectively none. No shikhara, no gopuram. The Rang Mahal is a small flat-roofed or low-domed chamber; the larger shrines in the compound have small domes/finials at most. Anyone modelling a tower here would be inventing it.
temples.facade: Plain. Plastered walls, simple rectangular or segmental-arched openings, metal grille gates and railings (much of the interior is fenced off from the public), painted panels and painted text boards. There is no documented carved stone, jali or columned facade at Nidhivan. The visual richness is vegetal, not architectural.
temples.entrance: A gate off a narrow lane, with shoe-deposit and flower-and-prasad stalls immediately outside, and a paved path leading in. No torana, no monumental gateway is documented.
temples.roofline: Low and incidental — parapets, a few small domes and kalasha finials, saffron flags on poles. The dominant skyline is branches.
temples.compound: Yes — walled and gated, and famously cleared and LOCKED at dusk after the evening aarti; no one, including residents overlooking it, is meant to remain. The grove vastly outweighs the buildings: shrines sit as small islands inside a dense thicket. Interior walls/paths are lined with railings that channel visitors.
temples.distinguishing: The trees. Wikipedia records that the bark is hollow, the ground dry, yet the trees stay green year-round; that every tree leans toward the ground; and that plants are found in pairs, their stems entwined. The grove is a low, dark, tangled, almost cage-like thicket — nothing like an ordinary wood. Second unmistakable element: the nightly ritual at Rang Mahal — priests lay a sandalwood bed, and set out bangles, flowers, clothes for Radha, tulsi leaves, neem twigs for tooth-cleaning, sweets, betel nut and leaf, and a jar of water, then everything is shut. Third: the lock-and-empty-at-dusk rule itself. For an immersive build, the entry sequence (narrow lane → stalls → gate → sudden dark low canopy → silence) is the whole effect.
temples.interior: Rang Mahal: a single small chamber, not a hall. A bed is kept inside and dressed with flowers by the priest each evening. No pillared mandapa, no processional axis, no documented pillar order. Lighting is dim — grove shade outside, lamp/low electric light inside. Other named elements inside the compound per Wikipedia: Sri Bansichori Radharani temple, a shrine to Swami Haridas, the Raas Lila Sthali (the dance ground), and Lalita Pond/kund.
temples.deityDescription: Rang Mahal holds no permanently displayed public murti in the ordinary sense — it is a shringar-ghar / resting chamber, and what is 'installed' is the dressed bed and the ornaments set out nightly. The Banke Bihari murti that was worshipped here (as Kunj Bihari) is now at the Banke Bihari temple. The Bansi Chor Radharani shrine and the Swami Haridas shrine hold their own images; their form, colour and dress are NOT documented in any source I could verify. Do not invent murtis for Nidhivan.
temples.confidence: medium
temples.sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nidhivan,_Vrindavan (grove character, tree behaviour, nightly bed ritual, Bansichori/Haridas/Raas Sthali/Lalita Pond); srimandir.com Nidhivan Mandir (Rang Mahal as marble shringar-ghar with bed); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banke_Bihari_Temple (Haridas, Nidhivan origin, temple 1862); mathuratour.com (12-acre figure, Gopinath Bagh); vrindavanmathuraguide.com (low hollow intertwining trees, uneven paths, locked at dusk). Materials, dimensions and shrine facades are largely undocumented in text — marked accordingly.

temples.name: Seva Kunj (Nikunj Van), Kunj Gali, off Radha Vallabh Temple Road, Gautam Nagar
temples.material: Walled grove with masonry boundary walls, plastered and PAINTED with murals; paved paths; a small shrine (Rang Mahal) carrying a white dome. Wall and shrine materials are plastered brick/masonry rather than dressed stone as far as documented. Lalita Kund is a masonry stepped well/tank — its stone type is not documented.
temples.primaryColour: Green canopy over cream/white plastered walls; the walls themselves are the colour event — covered in multi-coloured figurative murals of Radha–Krishna lila with inscribed shlokas.
temples.accentColour: Mural palette: blue-black Krishna, gold-yellow pitambara, red and pink for Radha and the sakhis, green foliage, ochre ground; saffron flags; white dome.
temples.approxFootprintM: Not documented. It is a compact walled block in the dense old-town lane fabric between Banke Bihari and Radha Vallabh — an urban kunj, clearly smaller than Nidhivan, and read on the ground as a walled garden you cross in a couple of minutes rather than a park. Do not publish a figure; measure from satellite imagery instead.
temples.builtYear: Site treated as immemorial lila-sthali. The present walls, murals, paving and landscaping are modern: the Braj Foundation lists Seva Kunj (Vrindavan) among the sites it has restored and beautified, so much of what a visitor sees today is 21st-century restoration work.
temples.towerForm: A single small white DOME over the shrine — that is the only vertical form. No shikhara, no gopuram, no curvilinear tower.
temples.facade: The mural-covered boundary and shrine walls are the facade. Painted panels of the leelas plus inscribed verses. Simple openings, metal grilles and gates. No documented carved stone bands, jali or columned arcade.
temples.entrance: Gate off Kunj Gali / Radha Vallabh Temple Road, immediately adjacent to the Radha Vallabh temple approach, opening into the walled garden. Free entry, two sessions (morning and evening). No torana documented.
temples.roofline: Low parapets over the enclosing walls; the white shrine dome with a finial; flagpoles. Nothing tall.
temples.compound: Fully walled and gated; garden/grove dominates and the shrine sits within it. Closes after the evening aarti for the same reason as Nidhivan — the belief that Radha and Krishna remain there through the night.
temples.distinguishing: A visitor's two-line answer: the white-domed little shrine in a walled tulsi grove whose walls are painted end-to-end with Radha–Krishna leela murals and scriptural verses; and Lalita Kund, the well Krishna is said to have drawn water from with his flute for Lalita Sakhi during the Rasa. Like Nidhivan the tulsi stems entwine in pairs. It sits inside the tightest, busiest lane network in Vrindavan — the contrast between crowded gali and quiet green enclosure is the experience.
temples.interior: No temple hall in the architectural sense. Open garden, paths, seating edges, the kund, and the small domed shrine containing painted decoration. Lighting: open sky over the garden, shade under the thicket, lamp-lit shrine interior.
temples.deityDescription: Not documented in any source I could verify. The shrine's interior is described only as decorated with paintings of Radha and Krishna's love. No murti form, material, colour or dress is on record — do not model a specific deity here without a photograph.
temples.confidence: low
temples.sources: vrindavanmathuraguide.com/mathura-vrindavan-temples/seva-kunj (walled grove, Rang Mahal at centre, Lalita Kund, murals on walls, tulsi in pairs, two sessions, closes at dusk); sanatanitraveller.com Seva Kunj ("small temple with a beautiful white dome", walls with paintings and inscribed shlokas, Kunj Gali / Radha Vallabh Temple Road location); brajfoundation.org /what-we-do (Seva Kunj listed among restored/beautified sites). Dimensions and deity undocumented.

temples.name: Keshi Ghat, Yamuna riverfront, Vrindavan
temples.material: Dressed SANDSTONE — the sources describe carved sandstone buildings and walls of red sandstone in Rajasthani manner, with stone-inlaid palace fronts. Expect the local Bharatpur/Karauli red-to-buff sandstone family, heavily weathered, water-stained and lichen-darkened at the lower courses, with later lime plaster and paint patched over parts of the upper storeys.
temples.primaryColour: Warm red-to-ochre sandstone, dulled by river damp to grey-brown at the bottom and bleached gold at the top; the sources specifically note the whole front turning gold at sunrise and sunset.
temples.accentColour: Lime-white and ochre-yellow painted render on later storeys; saffron flags; the dark red sandstone spire of Madan Mohan on the skyline behind; and the greenish Yamuna water.
temples.approxFootprintM: A continuous riverfront terrace rather than a building — of the order of 150–250 m of frontage, with the stepped apron running down to the water and the palatial fronts set behind it. No surveyed dimensions are published. The one hard document is an 1823 plan-and-elevation drawing on linen, 820 × 735 mm (Drawing Matter Collection, DMC 1675), showing a public bath at the centre of the ghat with an interior COURTYARD flanked by what are taken to be bathing rooms, plus the steps and the Yamuna (shaded blue).
temples.builtYear: 17th century, attributed to Queen Lakshmi Devi of Bharatpur; other accounts credit 18th-century Jaipur rulers for the carved sandstone buildings, arched corridors and domes along it. Sources genuinely conflict on patron and century — model the fabric, not the attribution. The 1823 survey drawing proves the developed bath complex existed by then.
temples.towerForm: The ghat itself has no tower. Its skyline is made of DOMES and chhatris. The tower in the view is the Radha Madan Mohan temple behind and above it — nagara, red sandstone, oval-profile, about 50 ft / ~15–20 m, on its hill by the river — plus the Jugal Kishore temple close by. That silhouette is inseparable from Keshi Ghat in every description.
temples.facade: This is the richest facade in the list and the best documented. The 1823 drawing shows TREFOIL and CINQUEFOIL arches (i.e. cusped/multifoil, three- and five-lobed) carried on columns, laid out across the elevation. Written descriptions add: tall pillars, arched corridors/arcades, balconies (jharokha-type projections) and intricately designed domes, with stone-inlaid palace fronts. So: an arcaded, multi-storey palace-front wall of cusped arches and columned galleries, with projecting balconies, rising straight out of the stepped bank.
temples.entrance: You arrive down through the lanes and onto the terrace from behind/above; the ghat's real 'entrance' is the flight of ornately carved stone STEPS running the full width down into the Yamuna, used for bathing and for boarding boats. Boats moor at the foot of the steps.
temples.roofline: Domes and chhatris (domed pavilions on slender columns), parapets between them, finials, and saffron flags. Note for accuracy: across Vrindavan generally, ground levels have risen and at several ghats only the chhatris now stand above buried steps — Keshi Ghat is the one main ghat still substantially functioning.
temples.compound: No compound — it is public riverfront. The relationship is inverted from a temple: a long open stepped terrace with the town's back wall of palaces above it, the river in front, and the parikrama marg passing along the top. Chir Ghat lies a little west, Kaliya Ghat and Madan Mohan a short walk on.
temples.distinguishing: The one postcard of Vrindavan: a tall red-sandstone Rajasthani palace front of cusped arches, balconies and domes rising directly from broad carved steps into the Yamuna, with the Madan Mohan spire on its hill behind, wooden boats at the water's edge, turtles and fish in the shallows, and the Yamuna maha-aarti performed here every evening with lamp trays, bells and crowds massed on the steps. Evening aarti is the set-piece — if a build wants one Vrindavan 'arrival' moment, this is it.
temples.interior: There is no temple interior. The interior condition documented is the 1823 bath complex: a central public bath with an enclosed courtyard, bathing rooms off it, and columned, cusped-arched galleries. Present-day interiors of the fronting buildings are not documented; many are occupied as ashrams, dharamshalas and residences.
temples.deityDescription: No presiding murti at the ghat itself. The associated deities are next door: Radha Madan Mohan (Krishna as Madan Mohan with Radha and Lalita flanking; originals moved to Karauli in 1670, replicas installed 1748) on the hill above the river, and Jugal Kishore nearby. The Yamuna herself is what is worshipped on the steps, by lamp aarti — no fixed image.
temples.confidence: high
temples.sources: drawingmatter.org/keshi-ghat (1823 ink-on-linen plan+elevation, 820×735 mm, DMC 1675; public bath, interior courtyard, bathing rooms, trefoil and cinquefoil arches on columns); vrindavancenter.org/history-of-keshi-ghat (stone-inlaid palaces on the banks, Madan Mohan in the backdrop, east of Chir Ghat); holidify.com and mathuravrindavantemples.com Keshi Ghat (Rajasthani style, tall pillars, domes, balconies, red sandstone walls, carved steps, Lakshmi Devi of Bharatpur 17th c., evening Yamuna maha-aarti); merobrajdham.com Keshi Ghat (carved sandstone buildings, arched corridors, domes, Jaipur rulers 18th c., golden light); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radha_Madan_Mohan_Temple,_Vrindavan (red sandstone, nagara, oval, 50 ft, hill by Yamuna, 1580/1819, deity arrangement); echoesoftime.co.in/ghats-of-vrindavan (32 ghats per gazetteer, burial of steps, chhatris left standing).

temples.name: Chir Ghat (Cheer Ghat), Vrindavan parikrama marg
temples.material: Almost no built architecture. A masonry/plaster walled enclosure and paved platform around an ancient kadamba tree, on the parikrama marg; the ghat's original stone steps survive only where not buried. No dressed-stone temple is documented here.
temples.primaryColour: The tree first — grey-brown bark, dense green canopy — then whitewashed/lime-plastered enclosure walls and grey stone paving.
temples.accentColour: The signature colour is fabric: women tie chunris and dupattas to the branches for wish-fulfilment, so the tree carries knots of red, pink, orange, yellow and green cloth. Plus saffron flags and marigold offerings.
temples.approxFootprintM: Small — a wayside enclosure around one tree and its platform, of the order of 15–30 m across. Not surveyed. The kadamba canopy is the tall element, roughly 10–15 m.
temples.builtYear: Site is a lila-sthali, not a dated monument. No construction date documented for the present enclosure or shrine.
temples.towerForm: None. Flat-roofed or open. Nothing rises here.
temples.facade: Plain plastered walls, gate/railing, painted name-boards in Hindi. No arches, jali, columns or carved bands documented.
temples.entrance: Directly off the parikrama marg through a gate or opening in the boundary; steps within the compound. No torana.
temples.roofline: Flat/parapeted, possibly a small canopy or shed roof over the murti near the tree. Flags. No chhatris documented.
temples.compound: A small walled wayside compound on the pilgrim circuit, with the tree occupying most of it. The critically accurate point: the Yamuna has MOVED. Chir Ghat was on the bank; it now stands some distance inland, so a correct model must NOT show water at its steps.
temples.distinguishing: One thing and one thing only: the ancient kadamba — the chir-kadamba / Ter Kadamb — held to be the tree Krishna climbed with the gopis' stolen clothes, still standing, still worshipped and given offerings, its branches hung with tied cloth. Add: this is where the gopis are said to have performed the Katyayani Vrata in Margashirsha, which ties it directly to the Katyayani Peeth in the same list. And the dry, inland, dusty condition of a 'ghat' with no river — that oddity is itself unmistakable.
temples.interior: No hall. An open compound with the tree, a platform and a small covered shrine niche.
temples.deityDescription: A BLACK murti of Krishna is reported as kept near the kadamba on which he hid the gopis' clothes. Its size, stone type, iconographic detail and dress are NOT documented — I found only the fact that it is black and stands by the tree. Model it small and shrine-scale, and do not invent attributes.
temples.confidence: low
temples.sources: brajrasik.org/articles/…/chir-ghat-or-cheer-ghat-vrindavan (ancient kadamba survives and is worshipped and given offerings; Yamuna has changed course and the ghat now stands away from the river); hindu-calendar.com Chir Ghat (black murti of Krishna kept near the kadamba; dupattas hung on the tree for wish fulfilment); harekrishnamandir.org Chir Ghat and thegaudiyatreasuresofbengal.com (gopis' Katyayani Vrata in Margashirsha here; located on the parikrama road just before Keshi Ghat); vrindavancenter.org (Keshi Ghat lies 'a little east of Chir-ghat'). No architectural survey of this site exists in text — hence low confidence.

temples.name: Kaliya Ghat / Kaliya Daha, Vrindavan parikrama marg, below Madan Mohan
temples.material: Again a site, not a monument: a stepped masonry ghat (now largely dry and partly buried), a platform and railing around a surviving kadamba tree, and — about 100 m away — the small Kaliya Mardana Krishna temple, a modest plastered masonry shrine. The red sandstone architecture in view belongs to Madan Mohan above, not to the ghat.
temples.primaryColour: Weathered grey-brown stonework and whitewashed plaster at ground level, green canopy over it, and the dark red sandstone mass of the Madan Mohan temple standing up on its hill immediately behind — that red-on-green is the colour signature of the place.
temples.accentColour: Saffron flags and cloth, vermilion on the shrine, marigold, and the ochre-white of the samadhi and bhajan kutir structures nearby.
temples.approxFootprintM: Small — the ghat frontage and tree platform together read as a few tens of metres; the Kaliya Mardana shrine is a single small chamber roughly 100 m off. No surveyed dimensions published. The kadamba is the tall element, roughly 12–18 m.
temples.builtYear: The present ghat fabric is undated in the sources. The Kaliya Mardana Krishna temple is traditionally ascribed to Vajranabha, Krishna's great-grandson — a devotional attribution, not an archaeological date; the standing structure is far later. Madan Mohan above it: rebuilt 1580 under Sanatana Goswami by Kapur Ram Das of Multan, and rebuilt again on the hill by Nanda Kumar Basu in 1819.
temples.towerForm: The ghat: none. The Kaliya Mardana shrine: a small shrine, tower form not documented — do not give it a shikhara without a photograph. The tower in every view is Madan Mohan's nagara spire on the hill, red sandstone, ~15–20 m (50 ft), oval-profile.
temples.facade: Plain plastered walls and railings at the ghat. Not documented in any richer detail.
temples.entrance: Off the parikrama marg, a three-minute walk from the Madan Mohan temple; steps down to what used to be the water.
temples.roofline: Low parapets, small domes/finials on the nearby samadhi structures, flags. The dominant roofline is borrowed from Madan Mohan above.
temples.compound: An open stretch of the pilgrim circuit rather than an enclosure. Immediately around it: the bhajan kutir and SAMADHI of Prabodhananda Saraswati, and the bhajan sthali of Bilvamangal Thakur — small memorial structures that give the strip its character.
temples.distinguishing: The hollow, still-living kadamba on the old bank — the tree Krishna is said to have climbed before leaping into the poisoned pool — surviving as the single tree that lived through Kaliya's poison. A visitor's description: a dry, sunken, half-buried ghat with the ancient hollow tree on it, the red spire of Madan Mohan looking down from the hill, and no river, because the Yamuna has shifted away. The dry-ghat condition is the honest and most recognisable fact about it.
temples.interior: No hall. The Kaliya Mardana temple is a single small garbhagriha-type chamber with limited darshan hours (roughly 7:00–12:30 and 17:00–19:30). Interior details are not documented.
temples.deityDescription: A deity of Kaliya-Mardana Krishna — Krishna dancing on the serpent's hoods — is recorded as installed at the temple, with the installation traditionally ascribed to Vajranabha. Its material, colour, size, number of serpent hoods and dress are NOT documented in anything I could verify. Model the iconography (Krishna dancing on Kaliya, flute or tail in hand) only as the standard Kaliya-mardana type, and flag it as a reconstruction.
temples.confidence: low
temples.sources: thegaudiyatreasuresofbengal.com/2023/05/21/krishnas-triumph-over-kaliya-at-kaliya-ghat-vrindavan/ (solitary surviving kadamba on the bank of Kaliya Daha, former series of steps down to the water, Yamuna has shifted away, Prabodhananda Saraswati's bhajan kutir and samadhi and Bilvamangal Thakur's bhajan sthali adjoining, on the parikrama marg a short walk from Radha Madan Mohan); tirthayatra.org/kaliya-ghat (kadamba hollow and still growing, Kaliya Mardana temple ~100 m away ascribed to Vajranabha, darshan timings); iskcondesiretree.com Kaliya Ghat; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radha_Madan_Mohan_Temple,_Vrindavan (red sandstone, nagara, 50 ft, hill near Yamuna, near Kaliya Ghat).

temples.name: Katyayani Peeth / Uma Shakti Peeth, Vrindavan
temples.material: WHITE MARBLE building with BLACK STONE pillars — this contrast is the documented and defining material fact. Rajasthani-influenced carving and painted work; gold-coloured (painted/gilded) lion sculptures at the entrance.
temples.primaryColour: White — a bright white marble mass, unusual among the red-sandstone and lime-washed fabric of old Vrindavan.
temples.accentColour: Black (the stone pillars), gold (the paired lion statues and gilded trim), plus red/pink cloth and gold ornament on the goddess, and the steady flame of a continuously burning jyoti.
temples.approxFootprintM: Not surveyed in any source. The complex is described as having a VAST courtyard for worship and ritual, plus five shrines, a gaushala and a Vedic school — so the walled compound is substantially larger than the shrine building. Model the shrine as the small object inside a big paved court, and take real dimensions off satellite imagery. The 15 m height is my estimate for a two-storey marble shrine of this type and is NOT documented.
temples.builtYear: 1923 (some sources say 1929), built by Yogiraj Swami Keshvanand Brahmachari, who identified and re-established the site. The Shakti Peeth tradition is ancient; the standing building is early 20th century — so this must NOT be modelled as a weathered medieval temple.
temples.towerForm: Not reliably documented. Sources describe the building and its pillars but never name a shikhara or dome. Given 1920s Rajasthani-influenced marble temple practice, a shikhara with kalasha is likely — but treat it as unverified and check a photograph before committing.
temples.facade: White marble walls with intricate carvings and painted work in Rajasthani idiom. Several PILLARS carry inscribed verses relating to Goddess Katyayani — carved text is a distinctive facade element here. Black stone columns read strongly against the white. Arch types, jali and balcony details are not documented.
temples.entrance: A flight of STEPS up to the main courtyard, flanked by two standing GOLD-COLOURED LIONS (Durga's vahana) — the single most quoted feature of the temple's approach. Gates behind them.
temples.roofline: Not documented beyond the general description. Do not invent chhatris. Saffron flags are normal for a Shakti Peeth but unconfirmed here.
temples.compound: Walled complex with a large open courtyard at its heart, the shrine building set within it, five sampradaya shrines around (Shakta, Shaiva, Vaishnava, Ganapatya, Saura — i.e. Katyayani, Shiva, Lakshmi-Narayan, Ganesh and Surya), a gaushala and a Vedic pathshala. Courtyard clearly outweighs the built mass.
temples.distinguishing: The gold lions on the steps against a white marble front with black pillars; the pillars inscribed with verses to the goddess; and the fact that it is a full Shakti Peeth — one of the 51, the Uma Peeth — sitting in the middle of Krishna's Vrindavan, with the sacred sword Uchhwal Chandrahaas enshrined and a perpetual flame burning. It also ties narratively to Chir Ghat, where the gopis are said to have kept the Katyayani Vrata.
temples.interior: Five separate shrines within one complex; black stone pillars carrying inscribed verses; a continuously burning jyoti; the sword Uchhwal Chandrahaas kept and worshipped alongside the goddess. Hall type, pillar count, bay arrangement and how the sanctum is framed are NOT documented. Lighting on the record is the lamp/jyoti plus daylight from the courtyard.
temples.deityDescription: Sources DISAGREE and I am flagging that rather than picking one. Some describe an ashtadhatu (eight-metal alloy) image brought from Bengal; others a black-stone image. Both accounts agree the goddess is MULTI-ARMED and SEATED ON A LOTUS. Standard Shakta dressing — silk, heavy gold or gilt ornament, floral garlands, a crown, vermilion — is normal but not specifically documented here. If the model must resolve it, an eight-metal (dark bronze-gold) multi-armed seated Katyayani on a lotus, richly draped, is the best-supported reading; label it as contested.
temples.confidence: medium
temples.sources: trawell.in Katyayani Shakti Peeth / Uma Shakti Peeth (white marble, huge black stone pillars, two gold-coloured standing lions adjacent to the steps to the main courtyard, 1923 by Yogiraj Swami Keshvanand Brahmachari, five shrines: Katyayani, Shiva, Lakshmi Narayan, Ganesh, Surya, sword Uchawal Chandrahaas); templepurohit.com Katyayani Peeth (Rajasthani influence, intricate carvings and paintings, pillars inscribed with verses to the goddess, vast courtyard); vrindavanmathuraguide.com Katyayani Peeth (white-marble building with black-stone pillars, gold lion statues, conflicting ashtadhatu-from-Bengal vs black-stone accounts, multi-armed goddess seated on a lotus, perpetual jyoti, five sampradaya shrines, gaushala, Vedic school, present structure modern).

temples.name: Imli Tala (Imlitala), Vrindavan parikrama marg, Yamuna bank
temples.material: A masonry temple building, plastered and finished, with walls carrying COLOURED BAS-RELIEFS; plus a small separate monument/protective structure sheltering the remains of the original tamarind and a newly planted successor tree. Specific stone or marble is not documented — do not assume red sandstone or Makrana marble here.
temples.primaryColour: Not documented with confidence. What IS documented is that the walls are polychrome — colourful, intricate bas-relief panels — so the building reads as a painted/coloured relief surface rather than bare stone.
temples.accentColour: The relief panels' own colouring; the golden complexion of the Chaitanya deity; saffron cloth; the green of the young tamarind.
temples.approxFootprintM: Not documented. A compact temple compound on the parikrama marg beside the Yamuna, with the tree-monument in its court. The 12 m height is my estimate for a temple of this class and is NOT sourced.
temples.builtYear: Not documented for the present structure. The site's fame is 16th century — Chaitanya Mahaprabhu is recorded as coming daily to chant under the tamarind here during his Vrindavan visit. The original tamarind has died; a new tree stands in its place and a small monument marks the spot. The standing 'magnificent temple' is modern Gaudiya construction; treat its date as unknown.
temples.towerForm: Not documented. Sources call it a magnificent temple but never describe a tower. Verify against a photograph before modelling a shikhara.
temples.facade: The documented feature is the wall treatment: colourful, intricate BAS-RELIEFS depicting scenes from the life and teachings of Chaitanya Mahaprabhu, running across the temple walls. That narrative relief band is the facade's identity. Arch type, jali, columns and balconies are not documented.
temples.entrance: Off the Vrindavan parikrama marg, on the Yamuna side. No gateway type documented.
temples.roofline: Not documented. Do not invent chhatris or kalashas.
temples.compound: A temple compound holding both the shrine and, separately, the small monument/enclosure over the original tamarind's remains with the replacement tree beside it. The tree-shrine is a distinct object in the court — that pairing is the layout.
temples.distinguishing: The name means 'under the tamarind', and the place IS the tree: a small protected monument over the stump/remains of the ancient imli, a young replacement tamarind, and a deity of Chaitanya Mahaprabhu seated beneath it — marking where he sat for hours with his japa-mala in the mood of Radha, and where Krishna is said to have sat meditating on Radha after she vanished from the Maharaas. Second identifier: the temple walls telling Chaitanya's life in coloured relief. Third: it stands right on the parikrama marg by the Yamuna, so the sequence of pilgrims passing is part of the scene.
temples.interior: Not documented beyond the deities present. No hall type, pillar arrangement or lighting is on record.
temples.deityDescription: Documented as installed: RADHA-GOPINATH, and NITAI-GAURANGA (Nityananda and Chaitanya) — the latter pair believed to have been worshipped by Sanatana Goswami himself. Separately, a deity of Chaitanya Mahaprabhu is seated at the monument beneath the new tamarind. Iconography of Gaura-Nitai is a fixed type — two standing figures with arms raised, Gauranga golden/fair, Nityananda fair-to-white — but the specific colour, material and dress of THESE images is not documented, so model the standard type and flag it. The narrative colour note from the tradition is that Chaitanya's golden form darkened here to the colour of a new monsoon cloud in separation from Krishna; that is theology, not a description of the murti's paint.
temples.confidence: low
temples.sources: thegaudiyatreasuresofbengal.com/2023/05/14/imlitala-temple-vrindavan… (original tamarind has died, new tree planted, protective structure and small monument to Chaitanya's visit, magnificent temple constructed, walls with colourful intricate bas-reliefs of Chaitanya's life, deities Radha-Gopinath and Nitai-Gauranga with the latter ascribed to Sanatana Goswami's worship, separate Chaitanya deity under the new tree, on the Yamuna bank on the parikrama marg); iskcondesiretree.com/page/imli-tala and bhagavatam-katha.com (Chaitanya chanting daily under the tree, golden form darkening); mathuravrindavantemples.com Imli Tala Ghat. Materials, dimensions, tower and roofline undocumented.

temples.name: Vamsi Vat (Banshi Vat / Vamshi Vata), Yamuna bank on the parikrama marg near Keshi Ghat
temples.material: A tree-site with minimal built fabric: a platform and small shrine/enclosure around a banyan on the riverside parikrama marg. No documented temple architecture, no documented stone. This is the least architecturally documented site in the list.
temples.primaryColour: Banyan grey-brown with its aerial roots, dark green canopy, over the dust-and-stone of the parikrama marg; whitewash on whatever small structure encloses it.
temples.accentColour: Saffron cloth and flags, vermilion, marigold; tied threads and cloth on the aerial roots are common at vat sites though not specifically documented here.
temples.approxFootprintM: Not documented. A wayside tree-shrine on the riverside path — of the order of 10–25 m across. Canopy of a mature banyan, roughly 12–20 m tall with a much wider spread.
temples.builtYear: No construction date. The important documented fact is DISCONTINUITY: the original banyan is said to have been carried away when the Yamuna flooded roughly 500 years ago; the tree standing now is a successor. So do not model a 5,000-year-old monster banyan as if unchanged.
temples.towerForm: None documented.
temples.facade: None documented.
temples.entrance: Directly off the parikrama marg on the Yamuna bank, near Keshi Ghat.
temples.roofline: None documented beyond a possible small canopy over the shrine.
temples.compound: None documented — an open point on the pilgrim route rather than an enclosure.
temples.distinguishing: This is the Maharaas site: the banyan (vat) under which Krishna as Gopinath played the flute (vamsi) on Sharad Purnima and the gopis, hearing it, ran to him — the single most celebrated event of the Vrindavan lila. Its unmistakability is entirely narrative and locational, not architectural: a big banyan on the river path a short way from Keshi Ghat, with the loss of the original deity to Jaipur and of the original tree to the river as part of the story. For a build, this is a mood beat and a landmark tree, not a building.
temples.interior: None documented.
temples.deityDescription: The Radha Gopinath deity historically associated with the Vamsi Vat site is NO LONGER HERE — it is in Jaipur (moved, as with several Vrindavan deities, during the 17th-century relocations). What, if anything, is installed at the site today is not documented in any source I could verify. Do not invent a murti for Vamsi Vat.
temples.confidence: low
temples.sources: brajrasik.org/articles/…/banshi-vat-or-vamshi-vata-vrindavan (vamsi = flute, vat = banyan; on the bank of Yamuna on the parikrama marg near Keshi Ghat; Maharaas on Sharad Purnima; Radha Gopinath deity now in Jaipur; original tree taken by a Yamuna flood about 500 years ago); thegaudiyatreasuresofbengal.com/2023/05/21/vamsi-banshi-vata-and-chir-ghat-vrindavan/ (riverside location on the parikrama marg; note this source is devotional and gives no physical detail). Both sources explicitly lack architectural description — flagged low.

temples.name: Yugal Ghat, Yamuna riverfront, Vrindavan
temples.builtYear: Not separately documented. Most of the Vrindavan ghats were built under royal patronage in the 16th-17th century; no source I found gives a date or a patron for this one specifically.
temples.material: NOT DOCUMENTED for this ghat. The Vrindavan riverfront ghats are generally dressed stone steps; do not assert a stone type for Yugal Ghat on my authority.
temples.primaryColour: NOT DOCUMENTED.
temples.accentColour: NOT DOCUMENTED.
temples.approxHeightM: n/a - a stepped riverfront, not a building.
temples.approxFootprintM: NOT DOCUMENTED. No survey figure found for width along the bank or depth of the flight.
temples.towerForm: None. A ghat, not a temple.
temples.facade: A flight of steps to the water. No facade documented.
temples.entrance: From the riverside lane onto the head of the steps.
temples.roofline: None.
temples.compound: None documented.
temples.distinguishing: THE NAME IS THE MEANING. "Yugal" is the Divine Couple, and the ghat is held to be a place where Radha and Krishna met with Their sakhis. What is documented is devotional rather than architectural: devotees sit on the steps and chant. Model it as steps and river, and do not invent a structure.
temples.interior: n/a
temples.deityDescription: No presiding murti documented at the ghat itself.
temples.confidence: LOW for anything physical. The sources are devotional descriptions, not surveys. Everything about its fabric, size and stone is unverified and is marked so.
temples.sources: vrindavanguide.com (Yugal Ghat; Ghats in Vrindavan) - devotional/tourist description, not a survey. General ghat-patronage dating from the same source and from tourist guides to the Mathura-Vrindavan ghats.

temples.name: Brahma Kund, Vrindavan
temples.builtYear: Renovated in the 1600s by Raja Bir Singh Deo of Orchha, who is recorded as the first to undertake its renovation. By 1882 it was reported to be in ruins.
temples.material: NOT DOCUMENTED. No source I checked names the stone or the lining of the tank.
temples.primaryColour: NOT DOCUMENTED.
temples.accentColour: NOT DOCUMENTED.
temples.approxFootprintM: NOT DOCUMENTED. No measured plan found.
temples.towerForm: None.
temples.facade: Stepped sides down to the water, with ghats on more than one side - the EASTERN GHAT of the kund is named in tradition. Nothing else about the fabric is documented.
temples.entrance: On the northern periphery of the Rangaji (Rangnath) temple, in the heart of the old town.
temples.roofline: None.
temples.compound: Not documented as walled. Its setting is the lanes around Rangaji.
temples.distinguishing: It is held to be the BRAHMA STHAN - the sanctum sanctorum of Vrindavan itself - which makes it the most revered site in the town while being physically modest. Tradition holds that Meera Bai spent her first night in Vrindavan on the eastern ghat of this kund. The documented arc is renovation in the 1600s and ruin by 1882, so a weathered and repaired tank rather than a pristine one.
temples.interior: n/a
temples.deityDescription: No presiding murti documented at the kund.
temples.confidence: MEDIUM for the history - the Bir Singh Deo renovation and the 1882 ruin are specific and repeated. LOW for anything physical: no dimensions, no stone, no plan.
temples.sources: The Braj Foundation (Brahma Kund, Vrindavan). Medium, "Tale of Vrindavan's sacred heart: Brahma Kund". Location relative to Rangnath temple corroborated separately.

temples.name: Chaar Dham, NH-44 and Bhaktivedanta Swami Marg, Chhatikara
temples.builtYear: Officially opened 8 February 2025, developed by the JC Chaudhary Trust. The site was previously known mainly for a Vaishno Devi cave replica, later expanded into the full complex.
temples.material: NOT DOCUMENTED. Modern construction; no source states the fabric.
temples.primaryColour: NOT DOCUMENTED beyond photographs.
temples.accentColour: NOT DOCUMENTED.
temples.approxHeightM: The two figures every source agrees on: a 141 ft (43 m) Maa Vaishno Devi and a 187 ft (57 m) trident.
temples.approxFootprintM: DISPUTED. One guide gives an 8-acre campus with landscaped gardens; the establishment's own site says 11 acres. 11 acres is about 211 m square. Treat as an estimate.
temples.towerForm: Not a single tower. The silhouette is the trident and the seated Devi, both free-standing, with shrine roofs below them.
temples.facade: Not documented.
temples.entrance: At the NH-44 / Bhaktivedanta Swami Marg junction, 629 m from Chhatikara Crossing - the first thing on the road into Vrindavan. Free entry. Darshan roughly 6am-1pm and 5-9.30pm.
temples.roofline: Not documented.
temples.compound: A walled campus with landscaped gardens, restrooms, seating, a canteen and a small museum section on the forms of Maa Durga.
temples.distinguishing: THE FOUR DHAMS HERE ARE NOT THE CLASSICAL FOUR. The establishment's own site names them SHIV DHAM, MAA VAISHNO DEVI DHAM, RADHA KRISHNA DHAM and SHANI DHAM. One guide site infers Badrinath/Dwarka/Puri/Rameshwaram; NO source states that, and it must not be built that way. The site's older identity is the VAISHNO DEVI CAVE, a walk-through, and it is still what most visitors come for.
temples.interior: The cave is a walk-through rather than a hall. Otherwise not documented.
temples.deityDescription: Shiv, Maa Vaishno Devi, Radha Krishna and Shani, one shrine each, per the establishment's own site. Iconographic detail beyond the 141 ft seated Devi on her lion is not documented - do not invent it.
temples.confidence: HIGH for the opening date, the trust, the two heights and the naming of the four dhams (the establishment's own site). MEDIUM for campus size, which two sources dispute. LOW for fabric and colour.
temples.sources: chaardham.in (the establishment's own site) for the four dhams and the 11-acre figure. vrindavanmathuraguide.com for the address, opening date, trust, 141 ft statue, 187 ft trident, 8-acre figure and timings. Coordinates 27.560892 N, 77.632279 E corroborated separately.
